# Modern Web Guidance (Source) This repo is the source repository for [GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance) and includes the code and documentation for authoring, calibrating, and evaluating its contents. [**Modern Web Guidance**](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/modern-web-guidance) is a set of skills that embed web platform expertise, best practices, and browser compatibility data directly into your coding agents. It helps to steer your coding agents away from legacy patterns, and instead toward solutions that harness the power and capabilities of the modern web platform. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](./CONTRIBUTING.md) and [GOVERNANCE.md](./GOVERNANCE.md) for how we work on the project and orientation of the codebase. --- *Stewarded by the Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, Mozilla Firefox, and MDN teams, alongside the web development community.* [Documentation](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/modern-web-guidance) · [Eval Dashboard](https://googlechrome.github.io/modern-web-guidance-src/) · [Source Code](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src) · [Report an Issue](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src/issues) ## Quickstart ```shell npx modern-web-guidance@latest install ``` This command runs an interactive wizard to install Modern Web Guidance. See [Alternative Installation Methods](#-alternative-installation-methods) below. #### Try it out (without installing) ```shell # Search for relevant guides npx modern-web-guidance@latest search "animate a dialog modal backdrop" # Retrieve a guide by ID npx modern-web-guidance@latest retrieve "animate-to-from-top-layer" # Scan a codebase for legacy patterns to modernize npx modern-web-guidance@latest legacy-scan . ``` ## Why? Coding agents often default to older patterns because LLM training data contains vast amounts of legacy code. This often leads them to generate bloated JavaScript for tasks that now have native, high-performance web platform solutions. Even if a model knows an API exists, it often lacks the density of real-world, modern implementation patterns required for production-ready code. **Modern Web Guidance bridges this gap.** Our skill's CLI returns targeted, expert-curated guidelines directly into your agent's context window, focusing on: * **Modern Browser APIs**: Helping models correctly structure APIs they frequently misuse. * **Performance & Accessibility**: Preferring platform-level APIs that can be optimized by the browser and include built-in accessibility affordances. * **Responsible Fallbacks**: Guiding models to use sensible, lightweight fallbacks instead of heavy polyfills or legacy libraries. ## What's Included? We cover the past several years of the web platform's new features, all the way up to the cutting edge. The guides are **designed to be token-efficient**; we run evals enabling us to prune lowest-common-denominator content that models already know. ### Core Disciplines

🎨 User Experience

Smooth visual states (View Transitions, entry/exit animations, parallax scroll, CSS scrollbar-color).

📐 CSS Layout

Modern layout systems (container queries, subgrid, modern color spaces like oklch, text-wrap tuning, and line-height trimming).

⚡ Performance

Speed optimizations (instant preloading, Interaction to Next Paint (INP) diagnostics, and scheduling tasks via scheduler.yield).

📝 Forms & UI

Native components (Anchor Positioning for tooltips, Popover API, dialogs, :user-invalid validation, and auto-sizing fields).

♿ Accessibility

Important considerations (screen reader and keyboard operability, content navigation and discoverability).

🤖 Built-in AI

Local client models (native translation, summarization, and language detection APIs).
_View an example:_ [the `navigation-drawer` guide](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/ui-components/navigation-drawer.md). #### The full list

**[optimize-script-priority](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/optimize-script-priority.md)**: Optimize the loading priority of scripts by boosting critical asynchronous scripts and deprioritizing non-essential or late-body scripts to improve sequencing and reduce delays. - **[out-of-order-html-streaming](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance/blob/main/skills/modern-web-guidance/guides/performance/out-of-order-html-streaming.md)**: Declaratively update a page with content streamed later into the same HTML document or via imperative JavaScript APIs. - ### Safe Adoption of Modern Features * **Progressive Enhancement & Nuanced Fallbacks**: We distinguish between purely additive enhancements (like speculative preloading) which are safe to let older browsers silently ignore, and critical behaviors (like dialog controls or network beacons) where we write highly considered, low-overhead fallbacks. * **Responsible Fallbacks**: We prioritize lightweight, case-specific custom fallbacks (<50 LOC) or conditionally-loaded polyfills instead of heavy third-party bundles. * **Gotchas & Quirks**: We document hidden platform limitations, such as the 64KB payload quota for `fetchLater()` or macOS-specific scrollbar behaviors. * **Baseline-Aware Integration**: We leverage real-time compatibility data from the **Baseline** project so agents dynamically adapt to current browser support. * **Origin Trial & Volatile Feature Gates**: Guides covering experimental **Origin Trial** APIs or **volatile features** (single-engine features shipped within the last 3 months or still stabilizing) remain discoverable via `search`, but are gated on `retrieve` so agents do not adopt unstable APIs without explicit developer consent. ### Project Configuration (`.mwgrc`) Configure Origin Trial and volatile feature opt-ins for a repository with an optional `.mwgrc` JSON file in your project root (or `~/.mwgrc` as a user-level fallback), which you can commit to share across your team: | CLI Command | `.mwgrc` Key | Effect | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | `npx modern-web-guidance@latest set-allow-origin-trials` | `"allowOriginTrials": true` | Unlocks guides for experimental Origin Trial APIs. | | `npx modern-web-guidance@latest set-allow-volatile-features` | `"allowVolatileFeatures": true` | Unlocks guides for volatile single-engine features. | ## How It Works 1. **Activation**: The coding agent activates the `modern-web-guidance` skill because of a relevant task. The agent is instructed to use the `modern-web-guidance` CLI for web platform queries. 2. **Local Semantic Search**: The agent runs `modern-web-guidance search ""`. The tool matches the query to the best guide using an offline, zero-dependency embedding model and BM25 search engine (no network calls, no API keys). 3. **Guide Fetch**: The agent retrieves the guide via `modern-web-guidance retrieve `, inserting targeted code patterns, gotchas, and fallbacks directly into its context window. > [!TIP] > Note: We use `npx` to ensure the content doesn't go stale, but the CLI works offline, completely private and local. > The npm package is self-contained, with no extra dependencies to ensure both low-latency and supply-chain security. ## Alternative Installation Methods
Vercel Skills CLI (aka npx skills) ```shell npx skills add GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance ```
GitHub CLI ```shell gh skill install GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance ```
Google Antigravity ```shell agy plugin install https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance ```
GitHub Copilot CLI ```shell /plugin marketplace add GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance /plugin install modern-web-guidance@googlechrome ```
Claude Code Plugin ```shell /plugin marketplace add GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance /plugin install modern-web-guidance@googlechrome /plugin # Select GoogleChrome marketplace, press enter, enable AutoUpdate /reload-plugins ```
Grok Build CLI ```shell grok plugin install https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance --trust ```
Kimi Code ```shell /plugins install https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance ```
OpenAI Codex ```shell codex plugin marketplace add GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance codex plugin add modern-web-guidance@googlechrome ```
## Updating If you installed the skill using `npx modern-web-guidance@latest install`, you can update with: `npx modern-web-guidance@latest update`.
Claude Code (if installed via claude-plugins-official) Anthropic stopped updating third-party plugins in their built-in `claude-plugins-official` marketplace on Oct 12, stranding installs at `v0.0.194` ([details](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src/issues/3533)). Switch to the `googlechrome` marketplace to get updates: ```shell /plugin uninstall modern-web-guidance@claude-plugins-official /plugin marketplace add GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance /plugin install modern-web-guidance@googlechrome /plugin # Select GoogleChrome marketplace, press enter, enable AutoUpdate /reload-plugins ```
Otherwise, consult your agent's documentation for updating plugins and skills. ## Evals to prove this works well We developed a robust eval harness to ensure that the content is **empirically proven and continuously calibrated** so AI agents write better code. We run automated evaluations using a closed-loop validation pipeline: ``` [ Expert-authored guidance and demo ] │ ▼ [ Target generation ] ──> Tasks on real webapps, Golden solutions, Playwright graders │ ▼ [ Calibration loop ] ───> Runs Grader on Golden Solutions (Must Pass 100%) │ Runs Grader on Unmodified Base App (Must Fail 100%) ▼ [ E2E agent evals ] ────> Runs coding agents in guided vs. unguided modes Compares pass rates and accessibility w/ and w/o the skill ``` 1. **Simulated Developer Tasks**: We define realistic developer prompts against full base applications (`daily-grind`, `devtools-times`) that mimic real-world requests (e.g., "make my images load faster"). Prompts avoid naming APIs or features, testing whether the agent can naturally discover and apply the right guides. 2. **Static & Browser-Based Checks**: Playwright graders verify that each implementation requirement was followed—checking source patterns, computed styles, runtime DOM behaviors, and accessibility states. 3. **Self-Healing Calibration**: Graders are calibrated against multi-agent (Claude/Codex/AGY) golden solutions (100% pass target) and an unmodified baseline application (0% pass target). 4. **E2E Testing**: We measure coding agent performance on real tasks with and without guidance. The _opportunity_ (100% - unguided pass rate) and _uplift_ (guided - unguided pass rate) are key: if models already succeed without guidance, we prune redundant advice; where agents struggle, we refine guides to maximize uplift. ### Recent eval results snapshot Explore full per-agent and per-guide breakdowns on the **[Eval Dashboard](https://googlechrome.github.io/modern-web-guidance-src/)**. | Date | Agent + Model | Tasks / Checks | Unguided → Guided (Uplift) | | :--- | :--- | :---: | :---: | | Nov 8 | antigravity_cli (gemini-4-argon) | 214 / 1673 | 58% → 94% (**+36pp**) | | Nov 8 | codex_cli (gpt-6.1-sol) | 215 / 1795 | 54% → 82% (**+28pp**) | | Nov 8 | claude_code (opus-5-5) | 215 / 1801 | 57% → 88% (**+31pp**) | | Nov 6 | codex_cli (gpt-6.1-sol) | 212 / 1773 | 53% → 86% (**+33pp**) | | Nov 6 | claude_code (opus-5-5) | 212 / 1773 | 56% → 90% (**+34pp**) | | Nov 6 | antigravity_cli (gemini-4-argon) | 212 / 1722 | 60% → 96% (**+36pp**) | | Nov 4 | codex_cli (gpt-6.1-sol) | 209 / 1743 | 52% → 85% (**+33pp**) | | Nov 4 | claude_code (opus-5-5) | 209 / 1743 | 57% → 90% (**+33pp**) | | Nov 4 | antigravity_cli (gemini-4-argon) | 207 / 1722 | 60% → 96% (**+36pp**) | | Nov 2 | codex_cli (gpt-6.1-sol) | 205 / 1729 | 55% → 82% (**+27pp**) | ## Available Skill Packs You can customize which skill packs are installed using the `--choose` flag: ```shell npx modern-web-guidance@latest install --choose ``` * **`modern-web-guidance`** (~205 tokens): Comprehensive guidance on modern browser APIs, layouts, and performance. * **`chrome-extensions`** (~175 tokens): Guidance on Manifest V3, background workers, extension APIs, and Chrome Web Store publishing. ## Telemetry & Privacy Google collects anonymous usage information to improve the tool's reliability, relevance, and performance. Collected information includes installation counts, the calling agent name, guide retrieval IDs, and CLI tool search queries generated by the agent (e.g. "dark mode scrollbar color-scheme"). Raw user prompts are not collected. You can inspect what is collected in [modern-web.ts](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src/blob/main/src/cli/modern-web.ts). > [!TIP] > **To Opt-Out:** set the `DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1` env variable in your shell profile (e.g., `.bashrc` or `.zshrc`): > ```bash > export DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 > ``` Google handles this data in accordance with the [Google Privacy Policy](https://policies.google.com/privacy). ## Contributors Found a bug, outdated pattern, or missing web platform feature? [Open an issue](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src/issues) or see [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) in the [source repository (`GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src`)](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src). Huge thanks to everyone who has contributed! ## License Unless otherwise noted: * Software code in this project is licensed under the [Apache License 2.0](https://github.com/GoogleChrome/modern-web-guidance-src/blob/main/LICENSE). * Documentation and guide content under `guides/` are licensed under [Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC-BY 4.0)](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Portions of the documentation in this project are derived from [MDN Web Docs](https://developer.mozilla.org/) by Mozilla Contributors and [W3C](https://www.w3.org/), [WHATWG](https://whatwg.org), and [IETF](https://www.ietf.org) specifications.

repositories.readme:

IMG.LY · CreativeEditor SDK
Sent.dm · messaging APIs for SMS, WhatsApp, and RCS

Become a sponsor

**Taste Skill** (`tasteskill 2.5.1`) is an Agent Skill that makes coding agents build professional company websites at the `figma.com` and `x.ai` level instead of assembling a generic landing page. Every build uses plain copy, one design system, one section per screen, equal left and right edges, real photographs (licensed stand-ins when the client has none), real brand icons and real product UI, a hero entrance and one or two dealt moments on every page, quiet micro-interactions, and shader effects and scroll scenes kept strictly for tech, gaming and software pages, all verified in a real browser by a checker and a finish gate that enforce the rules. Pages built from a single brief in earlier v2 runs:
The photographs are real, found in open archives and credited by the skill ([credits](examples/v2/CREDITS.md)). Watch the [launch film](https://github.com/Leonxlnx/taste-skill/releases/tag/v2.0.0). ## Install ```bash npx skills add https://github.com/Leonxlnx/taste-skill --skill "design-taste-frontend" ``` That installs the skill with the [`npx skills`](https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-skills) CLI. The skill runs its scripts with **Node 22+** and an installed **Chrome, Edge or Chromium** (set `CHROME_PATH` if it is in a non-standard place). Optional: **ffmpeg** on the PATH, for WebP output and the phone crop of a hero photograph in `photos.mjs`. It installs nothing and needs no API keys. Bundled Wikimedia Commons photographs work offline; fetching additional photographs or icons uses network access.
Claude Code plugin Run these inside Claude Code. The skill is namespaced under `taste-skill:`, so it does not collide with your other skills. ``` /plugin marketplace add Leonxlnx/taste-skill /plugin install taste-skill@taste-skill ``` `/plugin update` upgrades it later.
Codex plugin ```bash codex plugin marketplace add Leonxlnx/taste-skill codex plugin add taste-skill@taste-skill ``` Start a new Codex session afterwards so the skill is loaded.
From a clone, linked instead of copied `./install.sh` symlinks the skill into Claude Code (`--codex` for Codex, `--all-agents` for both), so a `git pull` updates it in place. On Windows (Git Bash) it makes a real link, or a directory junction when symlinks are not allowed, and it reports an older copied folder instead of skipping it silently.
Already have the skill? Run the install command again; the install name did not change. Looking for one of the older skills? See [Moved skills](#moved-skills). ## How 2.5 works Use it by asking your agent to build or redesign a company site; the agent loads the skill, copies `assets/` into the project, starts from `assets/starter.html` and runs the checker before it hands the page over. Every build starts by classifying the client's business (`software`, `gaming`, `tech`, `product`, `service` or `place`) and planning the page screen by screen before writing markup: 1. **Deal tokens and layout.** `scripts/start.mjs` deals a palette made for the trade and a Google Fonts pairing for the page kind (`library/palettes.json`, `library/type.json`), and `assets/layout/deal.mjs` deals a hero layout (`split`, `centred`, `product`, `photo`, `place`, `collage`, `editorial`, `word`, `film`, `statement` or `triptych`). 2. **Start from one system.** `assets/starter.html`, `assets/system.css` and `assets/layout/layout.css` enforce one section per screen at desktop (`1440x900`), equal left and right content edges, a fixed navigation bar and a single-screen closing footer (`footer.closing`). 3. **Show real product UI and real photographs.** Software and tech pages populate lit feature cards (`assets/ui/cards.css`) with rewritten HTML UI fragments (`assets/ui/`) and node-and-line diagrams (`assets/diagrams/`), with real brand and interface SVGs resolved locally by `scripts/icons.mjs`. Place, shop, hospitality and non-technical product pages lead with curated photographs (`scripts/photos.mjs`, `assets/photos/`), typography and flat colour, crediting sources in one expandable footer line with no captions under images. 4. **Keep effects for tech and gaming pages.** Shader grounds (`scripts/effects.mjs`), scroll scenes (`assets/scenes/`) and procedural 3D prints (`assets/objects/`) are dealt only on `software`, `tech` and `gaming` pages within a four-context WebGL cap, with static fallbacks for phones and reduced motion. Every page gets a hero entrance and one or two moments from `scripts/moments.mjs`; cafes, hotels, shops, studios and services get only the photo- and type-led ones, and zero WebGL. 5. **Check in a real browser over HTTP.** `scripts/consistency.mjs`, `assets/layout/check.mjs`, `scripts/perf.mjs` and `scripts/shoot.mjs` render the built page in headless Chrome across `1440`, `1024`, `768` and `390`, catching empty visuals, broken shaders, contrast drops, misaligned columns, section-height drift, placeholder text, invented street numbers and slow-network image gaps before the build ships. `scripts/gate.mjs` then holds the finish until no fixable FAIL is left, three rounds at most. Details of what changed from `2.1.x` are in the [changelog](CHANGELOG.md). ## The tools Everything is a plain Node 22+ script in the skill folder; none installs anything. | Tool | What it does | | --- | --- | | `scripts/start.mjs` | Deals a palette and a Google Fonts pairing for the page kind and prints the `` links and `:root` tokens. | | `assets/layout/deal.mjs` | Deals one of eleven tested hero layouts; `assets/layout/check.mjs` checks it with long-headline stress tests. | | `scripts/photos.mjs` | Deals vetted photographs by trade, enforces image weight and writes the one footer credit line. | | `scripts/icons.mjs` | Resolves real brand and interface icons into local SVG files. | | `scripts/effects.mjs`, `scripts/moments.mjs` | Deal shader grounds for tech, gaming and software pages, and the moments for every kind. | | `scripts/gate.mjs`, `scripts/copy-lint.mjs` | The finish gate (also a Stop hook) and the copy linter it runs. | | `scripts/consistency.mjs` | The checker: renders the page in headless Chrome over HTTP at `1440`, `1024`, `820`, `768` and `390` and prints PASS, WARN or FAIL per rule. | | `scripts/perf.mjs`, `scripts/shoot.mjs` | Page weight and speed, and full-page and per-section screenshots. | First run, from the project folder (a deal also arms the finish gate there): `node scripts/start.mjs deal --page software` (kinds: `software`, `gaming`, `tech`, `product`, `service`, `place`). Check a built page with `node scripts/consistency.mjs --page `. ## Moved skills This repo holds one skill, `design-taste-frontend`. The others moved to repos of their own and kept their install names: | Install name | Where it lives now | | --- | --- | | `high-end-visual-design`, `minimalist-ui`, `industrial-brutalist-ui`, `gpt-taste`, `stitch-design-taste`, `design-taste-frontend-v1`, `design-taste-frontend-v2-experimental` | **[Leonxlnx/taste-skill-classics](https://github.com/Leonxlnx/taste-skill-classics)** | | `imagegen-frontend-web`, `imagegen-frontend-mobile`, `brandkit`, `image-to-code` | **[Leonxlnx/imagegen-skills](https://github.com/Leonxlnx/imagegen-skills)** | | `redesign-existing-projects` | Part of `design-taste-frontend`, which audits an existing page in a real browser before changing anything | | `full-output-enforcement` | Removed. For the same problem, see **[Leonxlnx/unlazy](https://github.com/Leonxlnx/unlazy)** | Install a moved skill from its new repo under the same name: ```bash npx skills add https://github.com/Leonxlnx/taste-skill-classics --skill "high-end-visual-design" ``` ## Common Questions **What does the skill need?** Node 22 or newer and Chrome, Edge or Chromium; ffmpeg is optional (WebP photographs and the phone crop of a hero photograph). It installs nothing and uses no API keys. Bundled Commons photographs are stored locally; network access is used only when downloading additional photographs, Google Fonts or brand icons. **Where do the pictures come from, and can I use them?** From the skill's vetted photograph library (`assets/photos/photos.json`, including bundled Wikimedia Commons WebP sets and Unsplash photographs) dealt by `scripts/photos.mjs`. Library frames are used for trade and material details (or marked explicitly as draft stand-ins when the client has no photographs yet), never passed off as the client's own room, staff or product, and credited in one expandable footer line (`photos.mjs credits`). **Does it work with React, Vue, Svelte, plain HTML?** An empty folder gets a static page from `assets/starter.html`. An existing React, Vue, Svelte, Astro or Tailwind project is built in its own stack, with the kit served from its public folder; a Next.js brief is built as a static export. The browser checks run on the served or built page. **When does a page get shaders or scroll effects?** Shaders only on `software`, `tech` (technical hardware) and `gaming` pages, and always within a four-context WebGL budget with static phone and reduced-motion fallbacks. Places, shops, cafes, hotels, studios, services and everyday physical products stay calm: photographs, sharp typography and flat colour, with a hero entrance and one or two photo- or type-led moments in their own sections. ## Support the project If Taste Skill helps you, consider sponsoring: [Sponsor on GitHub](https://github.com/sponsors/Leonxlnx) ### Open Source Supporters

Get a Kimi API key: taste-skill users get 10% bonus API credits on their first purchase.
### Community Sponsors

Feedback: open an issue or pull request, DM [@lexnlin](https://x.com/lexnlin) or [@blueemi99](https://x.com/blueemi99), or email [hello@tasteskill.dev](mailto:hello@tasteskill.dev). Taste Skill has no official token, coin, or crypto project. Any token using my name, image, or project is unaffiliated and not endorsed by me. ## License [MIT License](LICENSE) · Copyright (c) 2026 Leonxlnx

repositories.description: OpenAI's Codex Security CLI and TypeScript SDK for finding, validating, and fixing security vulnerabilities. npm: https://www.npmjs.com/package/@openai/codex-security
repositories.readme:
# Codex Security

Codex Security helps you find, investigate, and fix vulnerabilities in your code.
Use its security workflows in Codex, or automate them with the
`@openai/codex-security` CLI and TypeScript SDK.

- **In Codex:** [choose a security workflow](docs/agent-workflows.md).
- **In a terminal:** [install the CLI and scan your repository](#quick-start).
- **In automation:** use the [TypeScript SDK](#typescript-sdk) or
  [GitHub Action](#github-actions).

## Features

- Scan repositories, selected paths, or Git changes. Deep scans repeat Standard scans and return their deduplicated findings.
- Validate candidate findings, generate patches, and verify existing fixes.
- Draft `SECURITY.md` policies and save threat models for later review.
- Browse saved scans and findings, identify duplicates, assess severity against
  your own rubric, and suggest owners from source and Git history.
- Preview third-party scanner findings, save them locally, or publish supported reports to Codex Security Cloud. [Scanner import guides](docs/scanner-imports/README.md).
- Track findings in Linear, Jira, or GitHub, publish completed scans, or export SARIF, JSON, and CSV. [Integration workflows](docs/plugin-connectors.md).
- Automate scans across repositories or project components, including in CI and
  containers.

## Use in Codex

Open your repository in a Codex session with the Codex Security plugin enabled,
then ask:

> Run a Codex Security scan on this repository, focusing on authentication and
> authorization. Return the saved report, source evidence, and coverage limits.

A completed scan saves a report and findings. Read the report for source
evidence and exclusions, then request a patch or ask Codex to verify an
existing fix. See the [agent workflow guide](docs/agent-workflows.md) for setup,
task selection, and recovery.

## Quick start

Requires Node.js 22.13.0+ within 22.x, or Node.js 24.x or 26.x, and Python 3.10+.
Python 3.10 also requires `tomli`.

Install the CLI globally and sign in:

```bash
npm install --global @openai/codex-security
cs login
```

Run your first scan from the repository directory:

```bash
cs scan .
```

When the scan completes, open the Markdown file at the **REPORT** path in the
terminal. Run `cs scans show` from the same repository to find its latest
completed scan again. See [scan scope and follow-up work](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#understand-scan-scope-and-follow-up-work)
for how to interpret exclusions in the report.

`cs` and `codex-security` run the same CLI. If the short name conflicts with
another command, use `codex-security`. To skip the global install, or if npm
reports an `EEXIST` conflict, use `npx @openai/codex-security` in place of
`cs` for both login and scanning.

For CI, set `OPENAI_API_KEY` or `CODEX_API_KEY` in the scan process's environment.
For a headless machine, see [device or SSH login](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#authentication).

### Scan options

Choose a scope and scan mode:

```bash
# Scan selected paths.
cs scan . --path src --path tests

# Scan committed changes from a base revision to HEAD.
cs scan . --diff origin/main

# Run a deep scan of the repository.
cs scan . --mode deep
```

Use `cs scan . --max-time 15` for an advisory 15-minute Standard investigation
allowance. See [investigation time](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#set-investigation-time)
for timing semantics and Deep Scan limits.

Use `cs --help` to browse commands, or `cs scan --help`
for scan options, cost limits, and patching after a scan.

For an application spread across repositories, see
[review one system across repositories](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#review-one-system-across-repositories).
Use [bulk scans](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#bulk-scans) for independent repository
reviews in one resumable campaign.

Scans use existing root and component `SECURITY.md` guidance. To write or
revise it, see [Generate SECURITY.md](#generate-securitymd).

Some cybersecurity requests and protected findings require
[Trusted Access for Cyber](https://chatgpt.com/cyber). For accounts with Daybreak
access, see [Daybreak opt-in](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#daybreak-opt-in) for the
Codex toggle and [Cyber access programs](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#select-a-cyber-access-program)
to select a program explicitly.

## TypeScript SDK

Install the package locally in your TypeScript project:

```bash
npm install @openai/codex-security
```

Then import it:

```ts
import { CodexSecurity } from "@openai/codex-security";

const security = new CodexSecurity();

try {
  const result = await security.run("/path/to/repository");
  console.log(result.reportPath);
} finally {
  await security.close();
}
```

The [SDK guide](sdk/typescript/docs/sdk.md) includes deep-scan configuration,
validation, severity classification, owner suggestions, and result handling.

Linked Git worktrees share scan history and saved findings when they use the same
Codex Security state directory. Keep `CODEX_SECURITY_STATE_DIR` stable to retain
that shared history and sign-in scope. See the [scan history guide](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#scan-history-and-reruns).

## Read existing Cloud findings

When Codex Security Cloud is available to your account, the Security plugin's
`$cloud-findings` skill can read findings, reports, recorded assignment and
verification, and scan status in Codex desktop or the Codex CLI. Cloud is an
optional connection; local scans work without it.

See [Cloud connection setup and CLI reads](sdk/typescript/docs/sdk.md#read-existing-cloud-findings)
for authentication requirements and a read-only example.

## Generate SECURITY.md

Use `policy` to draft a new `SECURITY.md` or update an existing one. Use `--path`
to select a component:

```bash
cs policy .
cs policy . --path services/api --knowledge-base architecture.md
```

The command saves its draft outside the repository and leaves existing files
unchanged. Review the diff and notes, edit the draft, then copy only `SECURITY.md`
to the displayed **Policy target**. Keep the saved architecture and threat-model
documents outside the repository.

Scans already use root and component `SECURITY.md` files. Keep your current policy
if it needs no changes. When updating it, preserve its vulnerability-reporting
instructions. If the command says the policy is already up to date, no copy is
needed.

Files at `.github/SECURITY.md` or `docs/SECURITY.md` often contain reporting
instructions. Preserve them when drafting a policy; those locations do not
automatically provide repository-wide scan guidance. See the
[policy guide](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#generate-a-security-policy) for policy
locations, unanswered questions, saved artifacts, and SDK usage.

## Save and export threat models

Scans and policy generation save threat models with their results. Export a saved
model without starting another analysis:

```bash
cs export --scan SCAN_ID --artifact threat-model --output threatmodel.md
```

Omit `--scan` to use the current repository's latest completed scan. The
[export guide](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#exports-and-ci) also covers findings,
SARIF output for CI, and the offline TypeScript API. For ServiceNow Application
Vulnerability Response, see [Export findings for ServiceNow](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#export-findings-for-servicenow).

## GitHub Actions

To run a weekly repository scan on GitHub-hosted Ubuntu:

1. Add an OpenAI API key as the repository secret `CODEX_SECURITY_API_KEY`.
2. Copy the [weekly workflow](github-action/examples/repository.yml) to
   `.github/workflows/codex-security.yml`. Replace `REPLACE_WITH_REVIEWED_COMMIT`
   with the reviewed distribution commit SHA from an Action release.
3. To try the workflow before the next scheduled run, open **Actions → Codex
   Security repository → Run workflow**.

The example uses an estimated $5 limit per scan and reports findings without
failing the job. Requests in progress can exceed the limit. For a severity
threshold, pull request checks, or runner requirements, see the
[Action guide](github-action/README.md). For eligible accounts, see
[Daybreak access](github-action/README.md#daybreak-access-and-refusals).

## Containerized bulk scans

Scan a list of repositories with the included Docker Compose configuration,
which keeps results and authentication between runs. See the
[container quick start](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#containerized-bulk-scans).
The [workflow runner](docker/README.md#workflow-runner) runs individual CLI stages
in containers and can connect to a separately deployed findings service.

## Findings storage and deduplication

The [findings guide](sdk/typescript/docs/findings-service.md) covers local
storage, deduplication, and compatibility with independently operated endpoints
through `publish scan --to custom` and explicit `--findings-url`. The local
`serve` command and browser dashboard have been removed; existing databases and
scan artifacts remain available.

## Other providers

Scans support OpenAI, Amazon Bedrock, OpenRouter, Fireworks AI, and Cheaper Inference. Bedrock uses
AWS credentials and does not require a separate OpenAI login. See
[Bedrock setup](docs/bedrock.md) for AWS profiles, regions, and model access.

For OpenRouter, Fireworks AI, and Cheaper Inference, set the provider's API key and choose a supported
model. See [provider configuration](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md#native-command-authentication-and-other-providers)
for examples.

## Documentation

- [Online documentation](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/security/cli)
- [Agent workflows and recovery](docs/agent-workflows.md)
- [CLI reference](sdk/typescript/docs/cli.md)
- [Imported finding identity and evidence](docs/scanner-imports/schema-guide.md)
- [Project configuration](docs/project-configuration.md)
- [Examples](examples/README.md)

To report a vulnerability privately, follow the [security policy](SECURITY.md).

# OpenBot ### AI coworkers. Ready for the enterprise. A modular, self-hostable workspace for AI coworkers.
Choose your models. Bring your agents. Own your infrastructure. [open.bot](https://open.bot) · [Docs](docs/README.md) · [Deploy on Kubernetes](#deploy-on-kubernetes) · [Run from source](#run-from-source) [![GitHub Trending: #3 Repository Of The Day](https://trendshift.io/api/badge/repositories/175080)](https://trendshift.io/repositories/175080) [![Trendshift: #3 Repository Of The Day](https://trendshift.io/api/badge/trendshift/repositories/175080/daily)](https://trendshift.io/repositories/175080)
[![Download for Mac (Apple silicon)](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/CopilotKit/OpenBot?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=3A3466&logo=data%3Aimage%2Fsvg%2Bxml%3Bbase64%2CPHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZpZXdCb3g9IjAgMCAyNCAyNCI%2BPHBhdGggZmlsbD0iI2ZmZiIgZD0iTTExIDNoMnYxMC4ybDMuNi0zLjZMMTggMTFsLTYgNi02LTYgMS40LTEuNCAzLjYgMy42ek01IDE5aDE0djJINXoiLz48L3N2Zz4%3D&label=Download%20for%20Mac%20%28Apple%20silicon%29&color=6E6AE0)](https://downloads.copilotkit.ai/latest/OpenBot-mac-arm64.dmg) [![Download for Mac (Intel)](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/CopilotKit/OpenBot?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=3A3466&logo=data%3Aimage%2Fsvg%2Bxml%3Bbase64%2CPHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZpZXdCb3g9IjAgMCAyNCAyNCI%2BPHBhdGggZmlsbD0iI2ZmZiIgZD0iTTExIDNoMnYxMC4ybDMuNi0zLjZMMTggMTFsLTYgNi02LTYgMS40LTEuNCAzLjYgMy42ek01IDE5aDE0djJINXoiLz48L3N2Zz4%3D&label=Download%20for%20Mac%20%28Intel%29&color=4A7CC8)](https://downloads.copilotkit.ai/latest/OpenBot-mac-x64.dmg) [![Download for Windows](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/CopilotKit/OpenBot?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=3A3466&logo=data%3Aimage%2Fsvg%2Bxml%3Bbase64%2CPHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZpZXdCb3g9IjAgMCAyNCAyNCI%2BPHBhdGggZmlsbD0iI2ZmZiIgZD0iTTExIDNoMnYxMC4ybDMuNi0zLjZMMTggMTFsLTYgNi02LTYgMS40LTEuNCAzLjYgMy42ek01IDE5aDE0djJINXoiLz48L3N2Zz4%3D&label=Download%20for%20Windows&color=9A5CC6)](https://downloads.copilotkit.ai/latest/OpenBot-windows-x64-setup.exe) Notarized .dmg for Apple silicon and Intel Macs · signed installer for Windows x64 · no terminal or developer tools needed · [Release notes](https://github.com/CopilotKit/OpenBot/releases/latest)
[![OpenBot for Business: get early access](https://img.shields.io/badge/OpenBot_for_Business-Get_early_access_%E2%86%92-D14B9C?style=for-the-badge&labelColor=3A3466)](https://dashboard.operations.copilotkit.ai/early-access/openbot?platform=business&ref=github&utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=openbot-early-access) From [CopilotKit](https://www.copilotkit.ai), creators of [AG-UI](https://github.com/ag-ui-protocol/ag-ui).
https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/c60f07da-8b6d-46eb-a573-17fc1e65a644

Watch a Bot use its browser and tools, answer with interactive results, and wait for your approval before it sends. Take over when it needs you, and connect the agents you already run.

## Getting started ### On your laptop The easiest way to get started is with the fully self-contained app that runs on your laptop, combining the OpenBot frontend and Docker-based backend in one application. [Mac / Apple silicon](https://downloads.copilotkit.ai/latest/OpenBot-mac-arm64.dmg) · [Mac / Intel](https://downloads.copilotkit.ai/latest/OpenBot-mac-x64.dmg) · [Windows](https://downloads.copilotkit.ai/latest/OpenBot-windows-x64-setup.exe) [Run from source](#run-from-source) ### For your team **OpenBot for Business** brings your agents into one workspace with company sign-in, tool permissions, approvals, and audit. Deploy on your infrastructure or work with our engineers on hosting and customization. [**Get early access to OpenBot for Business →**](https://dashboard.operations.copilotkit.ai/early-access/openbot?platform=business&ref=github&utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=openbot-early-access) · [**Talk to an engineer**](https://open.bot/business) · [**Kubernetes setup**](#deploy-on-kubernetes) ### Web, mobile, and chat [Web](https://dashboard.operations.copilotkit.ai/early-access/openbot?platform=web&ref=github&utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=openbot-early-access) · [iOS](https://dashboard.operations.copilotkit.ai/early-access/openbot?platform=ios&ref=github&utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=openbot-early-access) · [Android](https://dashboard.operations.copilotkit.ai/early-access/openbot?platform=android&ref=github&utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=openbot-early-access) · [Slack](https://dashboard.operations.copilotkit.ai/early-access/openbot?platform=slack&ref=github&utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=openbot-early-access) · [Teams](https://dashboard.operations.copilotkit.ai/early-access/openbot?platform=teams&ref=github&utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=openbot-early-access) ## Your workspace. Your stack.
- **Choose your models.** Use OpenAI, Claude, Gemini, or open models through an OpenAI-compatible endpoint, hosted by a provider or on your own infrastructure. Keep your provider relationships and change models as your needs change. - **Bring your agents.** Run built-in Bots in the OpenBot server, or connect your existing agents through AG-UI from any agent execution platform. Agents built with different stacks can work in the same workspace. - **Make it yours.** Use the MIT-licensed template as-is, white-label it, or customize it deeply. AG-UI connects agents, MCP connects tools, and the frontends and backend can evolve independently. - **Govern work across your team.** Company sign-in, roles, tool permissions, approvals, and audit apply across the workspace. Your agents use OpenBot's tools and computers under the same policies. - **Get help deploying it.** CopilotKit's engineers can work with your team to deploy OpenBot, connect your systems, and automate parts of specific jobs. [Connect your agent](#bring-your-own-agent) · [Configure models and tools](docs/configuration.md) · [Explore OpenBot for Business](https://open.bot/business) ## Built on CopilotKit and AG-UI OpenBot is built on [CopilotKit](https://www.copilotkit.ai), which is [used in production by a majority of Fortune 500 companies](https://www.copilotkit.ai/blog/series-a). **Your agent stack.** [AG-UI](https://docs.ag-ui.com/introduction#supported-integrations) has first-class integrations across the major agent frameworks and harnesses, including Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK, Microsoft Agent Framework and Agent Harness, Google ADK, AWS Strands, Oracle Agent Spec, LangChain, Mastra, Pydantic AI, Agno, and CrewAI. Many ship first-party support; [Amazon Bedrock AgentCore supports AG-UI directly](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-agui.html). **Your execution platform.** Keep your agents on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, Claude Managed Agents, [Google's Agent Platform](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform), LangChain's Managed Deep Agents, [Microsoft Foundry Agent Service](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/agents/concepts/hosted-agents), or your own infrastructure. Connect them to OpenBot through an AG-UI endpoint, using an adapter where needed. Your choice of agent platform stays independent of your workspace. ## Architecture OpenBot has three parts. On your laptop, setup runs the backend and Intelligence for you. For a team, the Helm chart deploys both on Kubernetes in your own infrastructure. | Part | What it does | | --- | --- | | **OpenBot frontends** | Mac, Windows, web, iOS, Android, Slack, and Teams connect people to the same workspace. Conversations, interactive results, computer view, and approvals adapt to each surface. [Choose a frontend](#getting-started). | | **OpenBot backend** | Runs the workspace API and built-in Bots, connects external agents and tools, manages Bot computers, and enforces identity, permissions, action policies, and audit. Deploys on Kubernetes with PostgreSQL and persistent storage. | | **CopilotKit Intelligence** | Durable conversations, memory, Automatic Learning, and enterprise governance services. Separately licensed; runs on Kubernetes alongside OpenBot. | OpenBot enforces sign-in, tool permissions, action policies, and audit at its API, alongside Intelligence's platform services. Built-in Bots run in the OpenBot server; your own agents can run alongside OpenBot or on any agent execution platform. Both use AG-UI and can share the same workspace. Computer execution is pluggable: use the default Kubernetes setup or connect a compatible external computer provider. [Architecture details](docs/architecture.md) · [Services and ports](#services-and-ports) · [Kubernetes deployment](#deploy-on-kubernetes) ## Open source, local operation, and licensing **The OpenBot application template is open source under the [MIT license](LICENSE).** You can fork, modify, and white-label it. It uses **CopilotKit Intelligence**, which is separately licensed and can run entirely on your own machine or infrastructure. | Where you run it | CopilotKit Intelligence license | | --- | --- | | **Your laptop, for personal use and experimentation** | Requires a free local Intelligence license. Desktop setup handles this for you. | | **Kubernetes evaluation** | Requires a free Intelligence trial license. [Request a trial](https://dashboard.operations.copilotkit.ai/early-access/openbot?platform=business&ref=github&utm_source=github&utm_medium=readme&utm_campaign=openbot-early-access). | | **Kubernetes / production** | Requires a production Intelligence license beyond evaluation. OpenBot for Business includes Intelligence for use with OpenBot. [Plans and pricing](https://open.bot/pricing). | **Fully local is an option.** Run OpenBot, Intelligence, and a compatible model locally. A cloud model or connected online app still sends requests to that service. Initial downloads, account sign-in, and local license renewal need internet access. --- ## Deploy on Kubernetes Deploy OpenBot and CopilotKit Intelligence together on **AWS EKS, Azure AKS, Google GKE, or your own Kubernetes cluster**. The chart installs Intelligence by default; no separate hosted project is required. For a first evaluation, you need a cluster with **amd64 nodes**, a **default StorageClass**, `kubectl`, Helm, a **trial or production license**, and a model key. The commands below use an OpenAI key. For Anthropic, a model router, cluster sizing, or an existing Intelligence deployment, use the full Helm guide that comes with the chart (`helm show readme` on the chart below). > **Setting up with an AI assistant?** Give it this README and the Helm guide (`helm show readme` on the chart below). The guide covers cloud-specific values, storage, secrets, sign-in, networking, upgrades, and troubleshooting. Use the evaluation below only through a local port-forward; configure sign-in and TLS before sharing a deployment. 1. **Create `openbot-values.yaml` locally.** Replace the placeholders with your license and model key. Keep this file out of source control. ```yaml config: singleUser: true postgresql: enabled: true secrets: licenseToken: "" modelApiKey: "" ``` 2. **Install** the chart published with the release. ```sh helm install openbot https://github.com/CopilotKit/OpenBot/releases/download/v1.0.2/openbot-0.2.0.tgz \ --namespace openbot --create-namespace \ --values openbot-values.yaml \ --timeout 15m ``` 3. **Open your evaluation.** ```sh kubectl -n openbot get pods,jobs kubectl -n openbot port-forward svc/openbot-server 3001:3001 ``` Open . This configuration is single-user: anyone who can reach it is an administrator. Keep the port-forward local. More at [open.bot](https://open.bot). ## Built on AG-UI A Bot is any endpoint speaking [AG-UI](https://github.com/ag-ui-protocol/ag-ui), the open protocol for agent-to-user interaction, so OpenBot is not tied to a framework and neither are you. Agents built with LangGraph, Mastra, CrewAI, Pydantic AI, Google ADK or written by hand all arrive the same way, and the governance rides the protocol rather than the framework. ## Main surfaces A Bot has eight things, always listed in this order: Conversations, Routines, Memory, Skills, Apps, Computer, Approvals and Activity. Tick Isolated on a Bot to give it a container of its own. Set `COMPUTER_RUNTIME=runsc` to run them under gVisor where the host supports it. - **A shell, not just a browser**: a Bot can run a command in its workspace, install what it needs, and process a file it saved. Through the same gate as everything else, so a rule can refuse a shell outright or refuse particular commands, and the command is on the record either way. The command inherits PATH, locale, terminal and proxy variables, not the rest of the deployment's environment. - **The gateway is the only way in**: it resolves the target from a server-held snapshot, evaluates the policy, writes the audit row, and only then calls the computer. There is no path that acts without the record existing first. - **CEL policy, fail closed**: rules can inspect `tool.name`, `intent`, `bot.id`, `actor.id`, `page.url`, `page.host`, `element.*`, `key`, `command`, `file.*`, `mcp.*` and `initiator.*` (what started the run, so a rule can refuse a scheduled routine what it would allow a person). Deny is evaluated before allow, a missing policy permits nothing, and a broken rule refuses rather than opens. - **Watch what it is doing**: the screen shows what a Bot is looking at, and the Activity list under it shows what it ran, read and saved in this conversation, with the output. A command line in the transcript opens to the same thing. A saved file shows its path and size, never its contents. - **Take the wheel**: a Bot that hits a login wall or a 2FA prompt asks for help. Control is handed over in the same panel and recorded as `computer.help_requested`, `computer.control_taken` and `computer.control_released`. While a person is driving, Bot actions are refused rather than queued. - **Secrets never enter the transcript**: the trail records that a secret was requested and how long it was, not what it said. - **Bring your own agent**: any AG-UI endpoint is a Bot, on a framework or hand-written. Endpoints are validated with the same target checks used for browser navigation, and an auth header is stored write-only. - **Components instead of prose**: compiled React components live in `app/src/components/gallery/`, sandboxed ones are authored in `/admin/playground` and published with no deployment. Every call asks the server whether the component exists, is published, and is not withheld from that Bot. Data functions are granted per component. - **Governed MCP**: Google Drive, Notion and the [public-web research providers](docs/web-research.md) Parallel, Exa and Firecrawl ship in the catalogue, and Composio brokers a few hundred more apps behind one account (Arcade can be the broker instead), each reached as the person asking. The catalogue carries only vendors this deployment stands behind, so adding one is a review of that vendor. Custom servers must pass URL checks; unknown tools and custom-server tools are treated as writes, and a catalogue tool the server advertises but does not name as a write classifies as a read. A Bot is told which connectors exist here and which it holds, so it says it has not been granted one rather than browsing to the vendor's website. - **Skills are instructions, not capabilities**: personal skills attach only to Bots their author owns, deployment skills are admin-owned, and both are invoked with `/` in the composer. A Bot granted the shipped `skill-creator` skill can write one with you in the conversation, and saves it only when you press the button on the card. - **Sign in with what your company already has**: Google, Microsoft or Okta from the environment, or a company's own SAML or OpenID Connect provider registered while the deployment runs and routed by email domain. Any one turns sign-in on; several may be configured at once. - **Decide who gets in**: `/admin/people` lists everybody who has signed in, promotes and demotes them, and removes access, which ends the session they are using and stops the next sign-in. Every change is on the audit trail. - **An audit trail you can read**: `/admin/audit` lists what was permitted, what was refused and what failed, and every refusal carries the rule that caused it. - **Credentials encrypted at rest**: stored through `/admin/credentials`, never returned by an API, and redacted from audit events. - **Loopback by default**: computers bind to `127.0.0.1` and require a per-container token, so nothing reaches a logged-in browser by knowing its port. The supervisor binds there too, because it holds the Docker socket and its token is a shared secret rather than a network boundary. - **Durable threads and memory**: conversations survive restarts through CopilotKit Intelligence, and each deployment stamps the threads it owns. - **Routines**: ask a Bot to do something on a schedule and it does, running as you, in the channel you asked in. A 15-minute floor and a cap of 20 enabled routines keep a sentence from scheduling more than a person meant, and ten failures in a row switch a routine off rather than burn model spend forever. Needs a worker process, which `scripts/start.sh` starts locally; see [docs/routines.md](docs/routines.md). ## Bring your own agent Any AG-UI endpoint can be a Bot. From `/bots`, create a Bot with: - name and instructions, which become its role description; - private or public visibility; - optional AG-UI endpoint, with the framework the agent is built on when it is one New Bot lists; - optional write-only authorization header. The server validates agent endpoints with the same target checks used for browser navigation, at registration and again on every redirect the endpoint answers with. If no custom endpoint is set, product-created coworkers use `MANAGED_AGENT_AG_UI_URL` when it is configured, and otherwise run in the OpenBot server on their role description. A private address is refused unless it is listed in `AGENT_ENDPOINT_ALLOWED_HOSTS`: ```sh AGENT_ENDPOINT_ALLOWED_HOSTS=agents.internal,10.0.0.42:9000 ``` A host on its own covers any port on that host; a host with a port pins that port. Matching is exact: no wildcards, no suffixes. An entry written as a URL, or containing `*`, stops startup and names that entry. The list covers agent endpoints only. Browsing is unaffected, the addresses holding a deployment's own cloud credentials are refused whatever is listed, and listing an address permits registering an agent there rather than granting that agent anything. Tenant package agents are declared in the package's own `agents.yaml`, in the directory `TENANT_PACKAGE_DIR` names (`examples/fintech` by default), or each in a file of its own under that package's `agents/` directory, as one of: - `built-in`, with a system prompt; - `remote-ag-ui`, with an endpoint; or - `remote-mastra`, with a Mastra server's address. More detail: [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md). ## Sign in `.env.example` ships `OPENBOT_SINGLE_USER=true`, which is one administrator and no sign-in: how a fresh clone reaches the product without registering an OAuth client first. Delete that line and configure **any one** of Google, Microsoft or Okta before anybody else can reach the deployment. With neither, it refuses to start rather than admitting everybody as an administrator. Configure more than one provider and the sign-in screen offers each of them. These four are needed whichever you pick: ```sh BETTER_AUTH_URL=http://localhost:3001 # where OAuth callbacks come back to BETTER_AUTH_SECRET= # openssl rand -base64 32 TRUSTED_ORIGINS=http://localhost:3010 # where the app is served from INITIAL_ADMIN_EMAILS=you@example.com # comma separated ``` Then the provider. Register the redirect URI shown beside it. ```sh # Google — http://localhost:3001/api/auth/callback/google GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID= GOOGLE_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET= # Microsoft — http://localhost:3001/api/auth/callback/microsoft MICROSOFT_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID= MICROSOFT_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET= MICROSOFT_OAUTH_TENANT_ID=common # your directory GUID for staff only # Okta — http://localhost:3001/api/auth/callback/okta OKTA_OAUTH_CLIENT_ID= OKTA_OAUTH_CLIENT_SECRET= OKTA_OAUTH_ISSUER=https://example.okta.com/oauth2/default ``` Restart. Accounts, sessions and roles are stored in the same PostgreSQL database as everything else. A company's own SAML or OpenID Connect provider is registered while the deployment runs, under Admin → Identity providers, and routed by email domain. An OIDC registration needs every host in the provider's discovery document listed in `TRUSTED_ORIGINS`, not only the issuer. - `INITIAL_ADMIN_EMAILS` is required, because it is what grants the first administrator. After that `/admin/people` can promote others, but an address named here stays an administrator and cannot be demoted or removed from that screen. It is re-read on every sign-in, so editing it takes effect the next time that person signs in. - `MICROSOFT_OAUTH_TENANT_ID` defaults to `common`, which admits personal Microsoft accounts as well as work ones. On a multi-tenant app registration Entra may send no `email` claim at all, so OpenBot falls back to `upn` and then `preferred_username`. If none of the three arrives the sign-in is refused and the reason is logged: add `email` as an optional claim, or use your directory GUID here. - A half-configured provider is refused at start-up rather than at somebody's first attempt to sign in: a client id with no secret, a `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` shorter than 32 characters, or an Okta issuer with no credentials behind it. - **SAML and OIDC** are registered while the deployment runs rather than configured here. Sign in as an administrator and go to Admin → Identity providers with the metadata your identity team gave you. People then sign in by typing their email address, and the domain decides which provider they are sent to. - **Put TLS in front of any deployment.** A page served over plain `http://` on anything but localhost is not a secure context, and sign-in cookies want `Secure`. ### Organization sign-in through another OpenBot A team deployment can leave sign-in to another OpenBot, the authority, configured with the Google, Microsoft or Okta settings above (your Kubernetes OpenBot can serve this role). Set `OPENBOT_ORGANIZATION_AUTH_URL=https://openbot.company.example` to the authority's origin. Use an HTTPS origin; HTTP is accepted only on loopback for local tests. Provider client secrets stay on that authority. The authority verifies the person and their current role; organization mode never substitutes `dev@openbot.local`, and it decides sign-in ahead of `OPENBOT_SINGLE_USER`. This optional URL is separate from `INTELLIGENCE_API_URL`, `INTELLIGENCE_GATEWAY_WS_URL` and `CPK_INTELLIGENCE_API_KEY`. Each deployment keeps its own Intelligence project credential. OpenBot Desktop does not offer organization sign-in. It installs the personal edition, which refuses `OPENBOT_ORGANIZATION_AUTH_URL`, and removes that setting from its `.env` on every Start. ## Keeping it to your machine - `agent-computer` drives a browser holding real logins. `docker-compose.yml` binds it to loopback; leave it there. - Store credentials through `/admin/credentials`, which encrypts them. Do not put credential values in tenant YAML or in committed files. - `AGENT_COMPUTER_ALLOW_PRIVATE_HOSTS` lets a Bot reach services on this machine. It ships commented out in `.env.example`, is for a laptop only, and a deployment running with `NODE_ENV=production` refuses to start while it is set. - To reach an agent on your own network from a deployment, list its address in `AGENT_ENDPOINT_ALLOWED_HOSTS` instead. That permits the one address, where the switch above permits the network. ## Development ```sh bun run format:check bun run lint bun run typecheck bun run test bun run build ``` After changing the Drizzle schema: ```sh bun run --filter server db:generate bun run --filter server db:migrate ``` Use `bash scripts/start.sh` for the whole stack and `bash scripts/stop.sh` to take it down. Use `bun run dev` only when you want the app and server without the Docker Bots and computers. ## Project status [![CI](https://github.com/CopilotKit/openbot/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/CopilotKit/openbot/actions/workflows/ci.yml) [![security](https://github.com/CopilotKit/openbot/actions/workflows/security_zizmor.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/CopilotKit/openbot/actions/workflows/security_zizmor.yml) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg)](./LICENSE) [![Latest OpenBot release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/CopilotKit/OpenBot?label=release&color=blue)](https://github.com/CopilotKit/OpenBot/releases/latest) ## Documentation - [open.bot](https://open.bot) - [docs/how-openbot-works.md](docs/how-openbot-works.md): a Bot's eight things, and where you set each one - [docs/README.md](docs/README.md) - [docs/architecture.md](docs/architecture.md) - [docs/configuration.md](docs/configuration.md) - [docs/personal-edition.md](docs/personal-edition.md): OpenBot for one person, with no sign-in and no Admin - [docs/development.md](docs/development.md) - [docs/coworkers.md](docs/coworkers.md) - [docs/routines.md](docs/routines.md) - [docs/automatic-learning.md](docs/automatic-learning.md) - [docs/deployment.md](docs/deployment.md) - The Helm chart, published with each release: `helm show readme` on it is the Helm guide - [docs/releasing.md](docs/releasing.md) - [docs/web-research.md](docs/web-research.md): public-web search and extraction through Parallel, Exa or Firecrawl ## Contributing - Open an issue or coordinate before starting substantial work. - Keep changes focused and update docs when setup, configuration, architecture, or user behavior changes. - Keep secrets, service-account JSON, customer data, and local transcripts out of the repository. - Run the checks in [Development](#development) before opening a pull request. ## License The OpenBot application source is [MIT-licensed](./LICENSE) © CopilotKit. repositories.name: ponytail
repositories.description: Makes your AI agent think like the laziest senior dev in the room. The best code is the code you never wrote.
repositories.readme:
Ponytail

He says nothing. He writes one line. It works.

Ponytail 5: rebuilt from the ground up.
-53% code · -41% time · -26% cost · -45% tokens
And yet: 98% of risky logic ships with a test. Without Ponytail: 68%.
Benchmarked in Claude Code, the same agent with and without the skill: 39 tasks including a real FastAPI + React repo, Opus 5.5, 5 runs each. Details.

Español · 한국어 · 简体中文 · 日本語

---

## Already built with Ponytail --- You know him. Long ponytail. Oval glasses. Has been at the company longer than the version control. You show him fifty lines; he looks at them, says nothing, and replaces them with one. Ponytail puts him inside your AI agent. ## Numbers

Two things the chart does not show: in a blind comparison, Ponytail 5's replies beat the previous Ponytail's 110 to 67. And on the six security tasks (SQL injection, path traversal, forged tokens, rate limiting, malformed CSV rows, caching) it passed all 30 runs: less code, no less safe. Method, per-task tables and limits: [benchmarks/results/2026-10-07-agentic.md](benchmarks/results/2026-10-07-agentic.md). **The rule was never "fewest tokens."** It is: write only what the task needs, and never cut validation, error handling, security, or accessibility. The code ends up small because it is necessary, not golfed. Lower cost and latency are a side effect. ## Before / after

You ask for a date picker. Without Ponytail, the agent installs a date picker library or builds a whole calendar by hand: 335 lines. Ponytail 5 first looks at what is already there: the repo has an `Input` component, and every browser has a date picker. It puts the two together. 10 lines. More survivors in [examples/](examples/). ## The review, rebuilt

`/ponytail-review` used to look only for code to cut. Now it reviews like the senior dev who gets paged when it breaks: it reads the code your change touches, not just the diff, and checks bugs, security, real load, missing tests, speed, and what to cut. Each finding says what the code does, what goes wrong, how to fix it, and what happens if you don't. ## The audit, rebuilt

`/ponytail-audit` runs the same checks on the whole repo. It maps the code first: entry points, how data moves, what load the project expects. Then it ranks what it finds and tells you what to fix first. The old audit only listed what to delete. ## New in 5.3: the band

In Claude Code, ponytail now shows a band above the prompt: what the current task costs, how many tokens and how much agent time it used, how often it reused existing code instead of writing new code, and whether the tests passed after the last change. Its buttons switch the level, run `/ponytail-review` or `/ponytail-audit`, copy the task as Markdown, and fold the band into one line. Don't want it? `/ponytail band` hides it, the same command brings it back. Needs Claude Code 2.1.290 or later, in the terminal or the desktop app. It does not show in the VS Code chat panel, cloud sessions or `claude -p`.

**Board** opens a local page with every task across your projects: cost, agent time and tokens over time, every session with its tests, and the days you worked. By default, everything stays on your machine, in `~/.config/ponytail/band/`. `/ponytail band import` adds your past Claude Code sessions to it, with their cost, agent time and tokens. ## How it works

The ladder runs *after* it understands the problem, not instead of it: it reads the code the change touches and traces the real flow before picking a rung. Lazy about the solution, never about reading. Lazy, not negligent: trust-boundary validation, data-loss handling, security, and accessibility are never on the chopping block. Logic with a branch, a loop, a parser, money or security leaves one small test behind. Every reply ends with what was skipped or not checked and any risk you should know. ## The prompt Ponytail is one prompt: [`skills/ponytail/SKILL.md`](skills/ponytail/SKILL.md). The compact version, for agents that read a rules file, is [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md). Everything else in this repo loads that prompt into different agents. ## Install **Claude Code**, as two separate prompts: ``` /plugin marketplace add DietrichGebert/ponytail ``` ``` /plugin install ponytail@ponytail ``` **Codex:** ```bash codex plugin marketplace add DietrichGebert/ponytail codex plugin add ponytail@ponytail ``` Then open `/hooks` in Codex, trust its two lifecycle hooks, and start a new thread. **Any other agent:** copy [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md) into your project, or ask your agent to install [`skills/ponytail/SKILL.md`](skills/ponytail/SKILL.md) as a skill. Step by step for Copilot, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini and the rest: **[INSTALL.md](INSTALL.md)**. That was it. He'd be proud. He won't say it. Active every session, with a handful of commands (see [Commands](#commands)). `/ponytail ultra` exists for when the codebase has wronged you personally. Startup and mode-change text shows the current mode. Only install ponytail from `DietrichGebert/ponytail` on GitHub or `@dietrichgebert/ponytail` on npm. It never ships `.exe` or `.dll` files; a copy that does is not mine. ## Commands | Command | What it does | |---------|--------------| | `/ponytail [lite \| full \| ultra \| off]` | Set the intensity, or turn it off. No argument switches ponytail on at the default level if it is off, and otherwise reports the current level. | | `/ponytail band [on \| off]` | Claude Code only: hide or show the band above the prompt. No argument switches it. The level stays. | | `/ponytail band import` | Claude Code only: add your past Claude Code sessions to the board, with their cost, agent time and tokens. | | `/ponytail-review` | Review the current diff like the senior dev who gets paged when it breaks: bugs, security, real load, risky code without a test, slow paths, and what to cut. Each finding says what the code does, what goes wrong, how to fix it, and what happens if you don't. Name a target in plain words to narrow or widen it: `uncommitted`, `staged`, `branch`, or a PR link. | | `/ponytail-audit` | The same check for the whole repo, most important first. | | `/ponytail-debt` | Harvest the `shortcut:` comments you've deferred into a ledger, so "later" doesn't become "never". | | `/ponytail-gain` | Show the measured impact scoreboard (less code, less cost, more speed) from the benchmark. | | `/ponytail-help` | Quick reference for the commands above. | Commands need a skill-capable host (Claude Code, Codex, Devin CLI, OpenCode, Gemini, Antigravity CLI, pi, Hermes Agent, Qoder, Grok Build). In Codex CLI and the IDE extension they're skills under the plugin's namespace; invoke with `$ponytail:ponytail-review`. Cursor with the [hooks](INSTALL.md#cursor) gets `/ponytail` level switching only, typed as a plain message. The instruction-only adapters (Cursor's rule file, Windsurf, Cline, Copilot, Kiro, Antigravity's `AGENTS.md` fallback) load the always-on ruleset without the commands. ## FAQ **Does it need a config file?** No. An optional `~/.config/ponytail/config.json` or `PONYTAIL_DEFAULT_MODE` env var can set the default level, but nothing is required. **Why does it write `shortcut:` comments?** They mark a deliberate shortcut and when to revisit it, and `/ponytail-debt` collects them into a ledger. Want another word, or none? Say so in your project's `CLAUDE.md` or `AGENTS.md`, then run `/ponytail-debt `. **What if I really need the 120-line cache class?** You don't. Insist anyway and he'll build it. Slowly. Correctly. While looking at you. **Does it scale?** The code you never wrote scales infinitely. Zero bugs, zero CVEs, 100% uptime since forever. **Why "ponytail"?** You know exactly why. ## Sponsors
