repositories.name: vorssaint-utils
repositories.description: Free and open-source macOS menu bar toolkit.
repositories.readme:
Vorssaint

One menu bar icon doing the job of a dozen paid Mac apps.
Install only what you use.

Website · Install · Features · Privacy · Changelog · Contact · Discord

For anything private, email hello@vorssaint.com.

Sponsors

Help keep Vorssaint free and open source. Share your product with Mac users.


Your product here
Your logo · Your name · Your link

Become our first sponsor →

Per app volume, a real system monitor, a better app switcher, window snapping, Dock previews, clipboard history, text snippets, a file shelf, an uninstaller. The utilities Mac users usually buy one by one, together behind a single menu bar icon, with no account, no telemetry and no subscription. ## Install only what you use Choose individual features or start with a preset. Uninstalled features stop loading and disappear from the interface; reinstalling restores their settings. Setup asks only for the permissions your choices need.

Reorder or hide panel sections, choose a compact layout, and export settings to another Mac or [keep them in your dotfiles](docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md#keeping-settings-in-your-dotfiles). The app supports more than a dozen languages. ## Everything it does ### Sound - **Volume mixer.** Set volume per app, boost quiet audio past 100%, and pin or reorder favorites. No audio driver required. - **Per app output.** Play music through speakers while a call uses your headset. - **Output switcher.** Switch audio outputs with a shortcut and lower the volume when headphones disconnect. - **Microphone tools.** Choose a preferred input, adjust its level on supported devices, and apply available microphone mute or input-volume controls with one shortcut. Siri and some apps may still hear you; Mic Mute is not a privacy lock. Its indicator shows that the feature is on, not that every app receives silence. - **Music app blocker.** Prevent unwanted Music launches after detected playback-button presses. Requires Accessibility. ### Know what your Mac is doing - **System monitor.** CPU, GPU, memory, temperatures, battery health and power use, with history graphs and a view of energy-hungry apps. - **Fan Control (beta).** Set manual fan speeds or temperature curves and monitor live RPM. - **Menu bar readouts.** Put your chosen readings, usage bars, battery time or fan speed directly in the menu bar. - **Network.** See live traffic, session totals and your local IP address, or run a speed test. - **Alerts.** Get notified about sustained CPU load, high temperatures, memory pressure, low disk space or low battery. ### Windows and the Dock - **App switcher.** Switch between apps and windows with live previews, search and display filters. A simpler mode works without screen capture. - **Window layout.** Snap windows into layouts, move them between displays and restore earlier positions using shortcuts, screen edges or modifier-drag gestures. - **Dock Preview.** Hover over Dock icons to preview windows across desktops. Switch, close, move or snap them from the preview. - **Dock clicks.** Click an active app's Dock icon to minimize, hide or cycle through its windows. - **Maximize windows.** Use the green button to fill the screen without creating another Space. - **Fixed Space order.** Keep Spaces in the order you set instead of rearranging them by recent use. Turning it off restores your previous setting. - **Quit on close.** Quit selected apps when their last window closes. - **Quit and close protection.** Prevent accidental ⌘Q or ⌘W with a hold, double press or extra modifier, per app.

### Keyboard and mouse - **Text snippets.** Expand short triggers into text with clipboard, date and time variables, or insert snippets from a searchable menu. - **Smooth scrolling.** Give your mouse wheel a fluid glide with adjustable speed and response. - **Pointer acceleration.** Disable mouse acceleration and restore your previous setting when turned off. - **Linear scrolling.** Make every mouse wheel notch scroll the same number of lines, however fast the wheel spins. - **Focus follows mouse.** Bring the window under the pointer forward after an adjustable pause. - **Scroll direction.** Invert vertical and horizontal mouse scrolling independently of the trackpad. - **Scroll sideways while holding a key.** Turn vertical wheel movement into horizontal scrolling while holding a chosen key. - **Side buttons.** Use mouse Back and Forward buttons in Finder, browsers and compatible apps. - **Mouse button shortcuts.** Assign keys to extra buttons and side wheels, or use button-drag gestures for Spaces and Mission Control. - **Middle click.** Turn a three-finger trackpad press into a middle click. - **Apps to leave alone.** Exclude chosen apps from mouse enhancements. - **Extra click filter.** Ignore accidental rapid clicks from worn mouse buttons without delaying normal clicks. - **Key debounce.** Filter repeated letters caused by a worn keyboard. - **Super key.** Use Caps Lock or a right-side modifier as a shortcut combination, with a separate tap action and app exclusions. - **Keyboard shortcuts.** Manage feature shortcuts in one place, including optional takeover of supported macOS shortcuts while a feature is active. ### Clipboard, files and links - **Clipboard history.** Search local text, image and file history, pin favorites, preview entries and paste with shortcuts. - **Auto clear clipboard.** Clear the system clipboard after a delay, sleep or lock, while keeping saved history. - **Paste as plain text.** Paste without formatting while preserving the original clipboard content. - **Shelf.** Park files, text and links near your cursor while dragging, then drop or share them later. - **Finder shortcuts.** Move files with ⌘X and ⌘V, rename with F2, or paste copied images as PNG files. - **Clean URL.** Remove tracking parameters from links, manually or automatically. - **Disk image installer.** Install an app from a mounted disk image and eject it, with optional download cleanup. ### Everyday tools - **Dynamic Island.** Keep music, notifications, calendars, timers, downloads and everyday controls around the camera cutout, or a simulated one on other Macs. Customize sections and shortcuts, with optional lyrics, a live equalizer, camera preview and file tools. - **AI agents.** Follow Claude, Codex, OpenCode and GitHub Copilot in the Dynamic Island: plan limits and when they reset where available, tokens, API value, models, projects and live work, with a notice when a long task finishes. Codex's banked resets can be used from there too, and each extra Codex account (`CODEX_HOME`) can have a limits card of its own. Copilot uses local CLI/app session logs; its token totals update when shutdown metrics arrive, and aggregate API-value estimates use base rates. - **Command Bar.** Search apps, windows, files, clipboard history, snippets and app menu commands from one field. Calculate, convert units, find emoji or run saved scripts. - **Quick panel.** Open a floating palette of favorite tools with ⌃⌘V. - **Quick toggles.** Switch appearance, hide desktop icons, eject disks, empty the Trash, lock the screen and more. - **Quit apps.** See every open app in one list and quit them one by one, all at once or all but the one in front. - **Radial menu.** Open a customizable wheel of apps, files, shortcuts and tools around the pointer, with profiles and submenus. - **Scratchpad.** Keep autosaved notes in tabs, with Markdown preview and export, in a floating window or Dynamic Island. - **Cleaning Mode.** Lock keyboard input while cleaning, with a black screen or a small visible indicator. ### Capture and create - **Screen capture.** Switch between screenshots, recording, text recognition and color picking in one selector with a pixel magnifier. - **Screenshot.** Capture an area, window, screen or scrolling page. Annotate, crop, redact, add backgrounds and watermarks, pin captures, send them through the Share menu or share an expiring link. - **Screen recording.** Record with separate system-audio and microphone tracks. Trim, cut, add automatic zooms, blur private details and export video or GIFs, or share an expiring link. - **Camera preview.** Check your camera in a floating mirror or Dynamic Island before a call. - **Copy text from screen.** Recognize text offline from any screen area, or read a QR code. - **Color picker.** Copy a screen color as HEX, RGB, HSL or SwiftUI code. - **Media tools.** Compress and edit videos, batch-convert images, add watermarks, make GIFs and extract text, all locally. ### App management - **App updates.** Check store apps, package-managed apps and supported developer feeds in one list. Install managed updates together or open an app's own updater. - **Cleaner.** Remove caches, logs and app leftovers, manually or on a schedule. - **Messaging downloads.** Review, organize or move messaging downloads to the Trash using retention rules. - **Uninstaller.** Remove apps and review their related caches, preferences and helpers before moving them to the Trash. - **Homebrew manager.** Search, install and remove formulae and casks without opening a terminal. - **Port manager.** Find processes listening on network ports and stop them with Kill Process when installed. ### Energy and display - **Keep awake.** Keep your Mac working on a timer, with the lid closed, or while selected apps, power or external displays are present. - **Displays.** Control individual displays and brightness, with hardware control where supported, half or quarter steps for the brightness keys, optional extra dimming below a monitor's minimum, software dimming as a fallback, and the volume and mute of a monitor's built-in speakers. - **Extra brightness.** Use a MacBook Pro XDR display's HDR headroom to go beyond its normal maximum brightness. - **Bluetooth on sleep.** Disconnect Bluetooth during sleep and restore it on wake only if Vorssaint turned it off. ## Install With [Homebrew](https://brew.sh): ```sh brew install --cask vorssaint ``` Or grab the disk image from the [releases page](https://github.com/vorssaint/vorssaint-utils/releases) and drag Vorssaint into Applications. Builds are signed with an Apple Developer ID and notarized, so macOS opens them without a fuss and your permissions survive updates. ## Uninstall With Homebrew: ```sh brew uninstall --cask vorssaint ``` To remove Vorssaint completely, including its settings and permissions: ```sh ./Tools/uninstall.sh ``` ## Private by default Vorssaint is local-first, with no account, analytics or tracking. The network is touched only by things you can see: update checks, the speed test, Homebrew actions, optional online lyric lookup, temporary screenshot or recording links and feedback you explicitly send. The full story is in the [privacy notes](docs/PRIVACY.md). Permissions get the same treatment. Every one is optional, the app explains each in plain words, shows which features actually use it, and even tells you when a permission you granted is no longer needed by anything, with a shortcut to revoke it.

See the [permissions guide](docs/PERMISSIONS.md) for which features need access and what remains available without it. ## What you need - A Mac with Apple Silicon - macOS 14 Sonoma or newer ### Build it yourself ```sh git clone https://github.com/vorssaint/vorssaint-utils.git cd vorssaint-utils ./build.sh --dev # build the separate Developer variant ./build.sh --dev --install # install and launch it ``` Xcode Command Line Tools are the only requirement. The [contributing guide](CONTRIBUTING.md) covers the layout and conventions. Official builds come only from the maintainer: the GPL covers the source, while the Vorssaint name, icon and look are covered by [TRADEMARKS.md](TRADEMARKS.md), so forks need their own identity. ## When something misbehaves See [troubleshooting](docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md) for launch problems, permissions and missing previews, or [support](SUPPORT.md) for help. ## Documentation - [Privacy](docs/PRIVACY.md), what does and does not leave your Mac - [Permissions](docs/PERMISSIONS.md), every macOS permission in plain words - [Troubleshooting](docs/TROUBLESHOOTING.md), the common fixes - [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md), build, layout and conventions - [Support](SUPPORT.md), where to get help - [Security](SECURITY.md), how to report a vulnerability ## Community Vorssaint went from first commit to the front of GitHub trending in three days, top of the Swift charts, and issues and pull requests have shaped every release since. Bug reports, feature ideas and translations are all welcome, starting from the [contributing guide](CONTRIBUTING.md). Vorssaint is free and will stay that way. If it earned its place in your menu bar, a star helps other people find it, and a [coffee](https://buymeacoffee.com/vorssaint) keeps the maintainer awake, with or without the Keep awake feature. ## Acknowledgements - App icon designed by [@divisionseven](https://github.com/divisionseven) ## License [GPL 3.0 or later](LICENSE), copyright 2026 Vorssaint. The license covers the source code; the Vorssaint name, logo and look are covered separately in [TRADEMARKS.md](TRADEMARKS.md).

Made by @vorssaint

repositories.name: rtk
repositories.description: CLI proxy that reduces LLM token consumption by 60-90% on common dev commands. Single Rust binary, zero dependencies
repositories.readme:
The cost reduction engine for AI coding agents.
Install it and forget it, then go as far as you want with pipelines.

Install • Pipelines • Docs • Website • RTK Pro • Discord

English • Francais • 中文 • 日本語 • 한국어 • Espanol • Português


**① Install & forget: up to 90% less command output.** Test runs, diffs, logs and builds are compressed before your agent reads them. 100+ commands, under 25 ms per command, no config, nothing changes in how you work. `rtk gain` shows what you saved. **② Go further with pipelines, as far as you take it.** Hand heavy reads to a cheaper model, compress more than bash, clean the API traffic without breaking the prompt cache. One agent-agnostic file: start from a built-in, install one someone shared, or write and share your own. The community built the bash compressor 85k developers starred. Now it is building pipelines: the best one listed today cuts total cost by 20.2% in its [author's benchmark](https://www.rtk-ai.app/pipelines/). **Agents across the whole company?** [RTK Pro](https://pro.rtk-ai.app) is the control layer for every AI agent: one gateway for every AI call, costs, secrets and personal data, policies, team catalog, audit. [Discover RTK Pro ↓](#agents-across-the-whole-company-know-what-they-cost-what-they-touch-and-who-ran-what)


---
## Install & forget **macOS, and Linux with Homebrew** ```bash brew install rtk ``` **Windows, with winget** ```bash winget install rtk-ai.rtk ``` **Linux, macOS or WSL, with the install script** ```bash curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rtk-ai/rtk/refs/heads/master/install.sh | sh ``` **Then plug it into your agent** ```bash rtk init -g # Claude Code; every other agent: see "Works in your agent" ``` Restart your agent. That's it: when it runs `git status`, RTK runs `rtk git status` and the agent reads a 3-line summary instead of 40 lines. Nothing to learn, nothing to call, and upgrading RTK never changes this. > Another project named "rtk" exists on crates.io. Check you have this one: `rtk gain` must show the savings dashboard, not "command not found". > > Cargo, pre-built binaries, native Windows, WSL and uninstall: **[Installation guide](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/getting-started/installation/)** · per-agent setup and `--dry-run`: **[Quick Start](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/getting-started/quick-start/)**
## Measure it: `rtk gain` Every command RTK touches is counted on your machine. One command shows what it saved, today and since you installed it. ```bash rtk gain # Summary stats rtk gain --graph # ASCII graph (last 30 days) rtk gain --history # Recent command history rtk gain --daily # Day-by-day breakdown rtk gain --all --format json # JSON export for dashboards rtk discover # Find missed savings opportunities rtk discover --all --since 7 # All projects, last 7 days rtk session # Show RTK adoption across recent sessions ``` **What the numbers mean.** The compressor reduces the **command output** your agent reads, which is one part of the input tokens, which are one part of the bill: a 90% cut in command output is not a 90% cut in cost. Token counts are estimated as `bytes / 4`, so the percentages are reliable and the absolute numbers are approximate. After a week of data, `rtk gain` ends with one line about RTK Pro, at most once a day and only on a terminal. `pro_hint = false` under `[display]` in `config.toml` turns it off. > Full explanation: [How RTK Savings Work](docs/guide/resources/savings-explained.md) · attribution, the live dashboard and export formats: **[Token Savings Analytics](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/analytics/gain/)**
## Out of the box: the bash compressor The part 85k developers starred. Built by 200+ contributors, written against real command output, and every filter has to cut at least 20% to ship.

| Operation | What the agent reads | |-----------|----------------------| | `cargo test` / `npm test` / `pytest` / `go test` | Failures only, with their assertion; passing tests collapsed to a count | | `git status` / `git diff` / `git log` | Compact status, reduced diff context, one line per commit | | `git add/commit/push` | A confirmation line instead of progress output | | `ls` / `tree` / `grep` / `rg` | Trees with counts, matches grouped by file, long lines cut | | `ruff check` / `eslint` / `cargo clippy` | Grouped by rule and file | | `docker ps` / `kubectl` | Essential fields only | 100+ commands across Git, GitHub CLI, Cargo/Rust, JavaScript (npm, pnpm, vitest, jest, tsc, Next.js, Angular, Playwright, Prisma), Python (ruff, pytest, mypy, pip), Go (go test, golangci-lint), Ruby, .NET, JVM (Gradle, Maven), PHP, Docker, Kubernetes, AWS, Terraform, and the file/search builtins. Every command and its filter: **[What RTK Optimizes](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/resources/what-rtk-covers/)** **Three promises** - **Never blocks.** If a filter fails, you get the raw output, and the command's exit code is passed through unchanged. - **Never worse.** RTK never prints more than the command did. - **Nothing hidden.** Output that is cut says where the full version is, and `rtk bypass` runs any command unfiltered, still tracked in `rtk gain`: ```bash rtk bypass git log --oneline -20 # full git log, no truncation rtk bypass npm install express # raw npm output ``` The hook rewrites shell commands. Built-in tools such as `Read`, `Grep` and `Glob` pass through untouched out of the box; in Claude Code, a pipeline compresses them too (see [Pipelines](#want-to-go-further-pipelines) below). > **Does RTK break the prompt cache?** No: output is filtered once, before it enters the conversation. [Details](docs/guide/resources/troubleshooting.md#does-rtk-break-claudes-prompt-cache).
## Want to go further? Pipelines. Out of the box, RTK compresses command output and stops there. A pipeline is how you ask it for more: one small file that tells RTK what to do with what your agent reads and sends. No file means the compressor above and nothing else; a pipeline adds one thing at a time, and you can take it back out.

**What people turn on first** - **Compress everything the agent reads**, not just shell output: grep results, web pages, lockfiles, any output RTK has no filter for (Claude Code). - **Hand big file reads to a cheaper model** you choose. The file never enters your agent's context (Claude Code, with your API key). - **Clean the API traffic** your agent re-sends every turn, with the prompt cache kept intact (through the optional proxy, below). - **Make the agent write less**: terse prose, with code, paths, commands and errors kept in full (every agent). Each of these is a built-in pipeline, one line to turn on. **[rtk-ai.app/pipelines](https://www.rtk-ai.app/pipelines/)** lists them next to the pipelines the community shares, each with what it saved and how that was measured. Installing one is a single command: ```bash rtk pipeline add github:user/repo # check and install a shared pipeline ``` A pipeline can rewrite commands and send content to the models it declares, so read its file before you install it. Written once, a pipeline works in every agent RTK supports, as far as that agent's hooks allow: **[Agent Coverage](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/resources/agent-coverage/)** shows what runs where. > Start here: **[Pipelines](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/pipelines/overview/)** · the built-ins, explained: **[Reference Pipelines](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/pipelines/reference-pipelines/)** · write and share your own: **[Writing a Pipeline](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/pipelines/writing-pipelines/)**, **[Pipeline Commands](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/pipelines/commands/)** ### RTK Proxy (optional) The `rtk-proxy` daemon runs the same pipeline on your agent's **provider-API traffic**: it strips bytes no model ever needed without breaking the prompt cache, and carries the calls your pipeline routes to cheaper models on the credential your agent already sends, so they show up in `rtk gain`. `rtk init -g` offers to set it up; `rtk claude` starts it and launches Claude through it with no configuration at all. ```bash rtk claude # start the daemon if needed, then launch Claude through it rtk llm-proxy status # is it up rtk gain # savings, command filtering and proxy side by side ``` Separate binary, separate licence (BUSL-1.1), its own `rtk-proxy-` archive: `rtk` never links it. Not the same thing as `rtk bypass`, which runs one local command unfiltered. > Setup and subcommands: **[RTK Proxy](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/proxy/overview/)** · what it compresses: **[What the Proxy Compresses](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/proxy/compression/)** · settings and endpoints: **[Proxy Configuration](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/proxy/configuration/)**
---
## Agents across the whole company? Know what they cost, what they touch, and who ran what. RTK runs on each developer's machine. **[RTK Pro](https://pro.rtk-ai.app)** connects them into one control layer for the whole company: - **Gateway.** Every AI call goes through one place, whichever provider each team uses. - **Cost control.** Spend by team, person and model. Waste found and removed. Budgets that warn, then stop. - **Shield.** Secrets and personal data masked before any model sees them. - **Policies.** Risky commands stopped before they run. - **Team catalog.** Skills, MCP servers and pipelines, assigned per team and project. - **Audit log.** Who did what, and whether it was allowed. Nothing changes for the developer. No secret value ever leaves the machine. The CLI stays free and open source. | **Just you?** | **Your team, or the whole company?** | |---|---| | The **Dev** plan: guardrails and analytics for one developer. Your own dashboard of spend per project and per model, the Shield and policies on your machine, nothing to administer. | **Teams**, **Business** and **Enterprise**: the full control layer for every developer, with SSO and the audit log, scaled across the organisation, up to on-premise deployment and a custom SLA. | | [Plans and what each includes →](https://pro.rtk-ai.app/pricing) | [See what it is worth for your team →](https://pro.rtk-ai.app/pricing) · [Talk to us →](https://pro.rtk-ai.app/contact) |
---
## Works in your agent RTK supports 18 AI coding tools. With a **hook** or **plugin**, `rtk init` installs it and compression is automatic. With a **rules file**, RTK asks the model to prefer `rtk` commands instead. | Tool | Install | How | |------|---------|-----| | **Claude Code** | `rtk init -g` | hook | | **GitHub Copilot** (VS Code, CLI) | `rtk init -g --copilot` | hook | | **Cursor** | `rtk init -g --agent cursor` | hook | | **Gemini CLI** | `rtk init -g --gemini` | hook | | **Codex** | `rtk init -g --codex` | hook | | **Mistral Vibe** | `rtk init -g --agent vibe` | hook | | **Factory Droid** | `rtk init -g --agent droid` | hook | | **Trae** | `rtk init --agent trae` (or `-g`) | hook | | **OpenCode** (1.18.29+) | `rtk init -g --opencode` | plugin | | **OpenClaw** | `openclaw plugins install ./openclaw` | plugin | | **Pi** / **Oh My Pi** | `rtk init -g --agent pi` / `--agent omp` | plugin | | **Hermes** | `rtk init --agent hermes` | plugin | | **Windsurf** | `rtk init -g --agent windsurf` | rules file | | **Cline / Roo Code** | `rtk init --agent cline` | rules file | | **Kilo Code** | `rtk init --agent kilocode` | rules file | | **Google Antigravity** | `rtk init --agent antigravity` (or `-g`) | rules file | | **Kimi AI** | `rtk init --agent kimi` | rules file | Per-agent setup, what each hook API allows, override controls: **[Supported Agents](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/getting-started/supported-agents/)** · **[Agent Coverage](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/resources/agent-coverage/)**
## Documentation **[rtk-ai.app/docs](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/)** is the full user guide. | | | |---|---| | [Installation](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/getting-started/installation/) | every install method, Windows, WSL, uninstall | | [Quick Start](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/getting-started/quick-start/) | per-agent init, `--dry-run`, first savings | | [Supported Agents](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/getting-started/supported-agents/) | setup detail, override controls, degradation | | [Agent Coverage](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/resources/agent-coverage/) | what each agent's hook API lets RTK do | | [What RTK Optimizes](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/resources/what-rtk-covers/) | every command and its filter | | [Configuration](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/getting-started/configuration/) | `config.toml`, env vars, recall recovery | | [Token Savings Analytics](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/analytics/gain/) | `rtk gain` in full | | [Pipelines](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/pipelines/overview/) | the engine: `pipeline.toml`, rules, judges, tasks, sharing | | [RTK Proxy](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/proxy/overview/) | the daemon: setup, what it compresses, settings | | [Editions and Licensing](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/resources/editions/) | what each download contains | | [Telemetry & Privacy](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/resources/telemetry/) | what is collected, how to opt in, your GDPR rights | | [Troubleshooting](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/resources/troubleshooting/) | common issues, prompt-cache questions | Repository references: [engine/README.md](engine/README.md) · [proxy/README.md](proxy/README.md) · [ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/contributing/ARCHITECTURE.md) · [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) · [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) RTK collects **no command content and no file contents**. Telemetry is anonymous and **off by default** — it sends nothing until you opt in with explicit consent (GDPR Art. 6 & 7) via `rtk telemetry enable`, and documented in [Telemetry & Privacy](https://www.rtk-ai.app/docs/resources/telemetry/).
## Editions and licence RTK ships as three downloads. The two `rtk` editions install a binary with the **same name** — hooks, scripts and agent config work unchanged across both — so they cannot be installed together. Uninstall one before installing the other. | Download | Licence | Contains | |---|---|---| | `rtk-` | Apache-2.0 + BUSL-1.1 | Hook core, every command filter, **and** the pipeline engine | | `rtk-oss-` | Apache-2.0 only | Hook core and every command filter. No engine. | | `rtk-proxy-` | BUSL-1.1 | The RTK Proxy daemon. Never bundled with either `rtk`. | **Production use is free**, engine and daemon included. What the BUSL grant does not cover is offering RTK or a derivative to third parties as a commercial product or service — for that, contact **contact@rtk-ai.app**. ```bash curl -fsSL .../install.sh | RTK_EDITION=oss sh # Apache-2.0 edition brew install rtk-ai/tap/rtk-oss ```

repositories.description: Open-source generative UI framework: agents stream layout data, and apps render it with native components in React, Angular, Lit, Flutter, SwiftUI and Jetpack Compose.
repositories.readme: # A2UI **Build delightful, fast, reliable agentic experiences** A2UI (Agent-to-User Interface) is an open-source generative UI framework, complete with a protocol optimized for streaming dynamic user interfaces at low latency, native renderers for web and mobile frameworks, and agent SDKs in several popular languages. With A2UI, your agents can communicate with your users using natively rendered widgets, in addition to text. _Examples of UI compositions that A2UI can express._ ## Quick links - [Main website](https://a2ui.org). - Try it in your browser using [A2UI Composer](https://a2ui-project.github.io/composer/). - [Supported renderers](https://a2ui.org/reference/renderers/). - [Supported agents](https://a2ui.org/reference/agents/). - [Protocol specification](https://a2ui.org/specification/v1.0-a2ui/). ## Introduction Large language models (LLMs) and decision models (e.g. [Jev](https://docs.typesafe.ai/)) excel at creating text and code and at making fast decisions on top of raw structured data (e.g. JSON). A2UI gives these models a specialized vocabulary for expressing user interfaces. A2UI expresses UI using _data_, not code. A schema for the data exchanged between the agent and the renderer enforces strict capability boundaries for the agent, keeping agent-generated experiences safe and aligned with the business requirements of your application. A _core library_, a _native framework adapter_, and a _catalog of components_ provide access to native components and form the building blocks that the agent _composes_ into a final user experience, making the result expressive and high-performance. ## When to use A2UI Use A2UI when any of the following apply to your application: - Parts of your application are agent- and/or server-driven. By design, A2UI supports remote rendering. - You want the UI to be composed dynamically, tailored to the user's immediate need. Instead of making your users navigate through multiple screens to solve their problems, have the agent build the right flow of UI that guides users directly to solutions. - You need the highest performance and visual fidelity. A2UI renders UI using the framework of your choice, typically one that the host app itself is written in. WebViews or HTML are not required. - The same agent streams UI to multiple platforms or frameworks, such as Flutter, React, SwiftUI, and Jetpack Compose. A2UI helps keep the user experience compatible and consistent across all screens. - The agent is remote, third-party, or operates across a trust boundary. For example, the agent must not be able to handle certain kinds of data (credit card/account numbers, PII, financial data). A2UI helps enforce the trust boundary and protect your app's critical functionality from hallucinations using a strict schema, and by expressing UI using validated data rather than executable code. ## A2UI core philosophy We develop A2UI under the guidance of the following core principles: - **Security first**: The app developer controls what the agent can and cannot do in the app. A2UI provides a framework for specifying and enforcing the necessary guardrails, such as expressing UI as data, validating inputs and outputs against a schema, and disallowing arbitrary executable code. Every capability granted to the agent is either a safe standard capability built into the framework, or a capability explicitly granted by the app developer. - **Model-friendly and server-driven**: The A2UI protocol is designed to be efficiently generated by language and decision models and transported over the network, and to support progressive rendering (or "streaming") for a responsive user experience. An agent can adapt the UI based on where the user takes the conversation. A2UI supports swappable inference formats, so you can tailor inference to specific models and use cases. - **Native rendering and portability**: A2UI renders UI using the framework native to your app, with renderers for many major UI frameworks. No need to change frameworks unless required for other reasons. ## Architecture A2UI's architecture is made of multiple layers spanning the full stack that connects the agent to the application: 1. **Inference**: An agent (typically backed by a language or a decision model) instructed by an A2UI skill (created using an A2UI Agent SDK) generates the description of UI and data using an appropriate inference format (e.g. A2UI Express, or a decision tree). 2. **Transport**: An A2UI Agent SDK, embedded in a larger agent architecture, parses and validates the model's output, expands macros, and converts the UI to the wire-stable _A2UI Transport_ protocol messages, which are sent to the renderer. 3. **Rendering**: A renderer is made of an _A2UI Core_ library (e.g. the `@a2ui/web_core` npm package, or `a2ui_core` Dart package), a UI framework adapter (e.g. `@a2ui/react` React adapter, or `a2ui_flutter` Flutter adapter), and a widget catalog. The core library parses the incoming messages and creates a framework-agnostic in-memory representation of the UI and data. The framework adapter maps the in-memory representation to concrete framework-specific UI widgets. The widget catalog provides access to the widgets the agent is allowed to compose. ## Getting started Pick the path that matches where you want to start: | Path | What you get | Time | | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------ | | 🍜 **[Quickstart](https://a2ui.org/quickstart/)** | A full-stack A2UI app with a backend and frontend. Learn A2UI end-to-end and customize to your use case. | ~5 min | | 🎨 **[A2UI Composer](https://a2ui-project.github.io/composer/)** | Generate A2UI JSON from a visual editor and paste it into any agent prompt — no install required. | ~1 min | | 🎬 **[A2UI Theater](https://a2ui-composer.ag-ui.com/theater)** | Step through pre-built A2UI streaming scenarios across Lit, React, and Angular renderers — no install required. | ~1 min | ## Packages These packages are developed in this repository. Packages marked "Not published yet" can be used from source. ### Python | Package | Description | Version | | ------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | [a2ui-core](python/a2ui_core/) | Protocol messages, data model, data binding, expression evaluation, and catalog validation. | [![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/a2ui-core.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/a2ui-core/) | | [a2ui-agent-sdk](python/a2ui_agent/) | Agent SDK: negotiates catalogs, generates prompts and skills, and compiles model output into A2UI. | [![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/a2ui-agent-sdk.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/a2ui-agent-sdk/) | | [a2ui-a2a](python/a2ui_a2a/) | Connects the agent SDK to the [Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol](https://a2a-protocol.org). | [![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/a2ui-a2a.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/a2ui-a2a/) | | [a2ui-adk](python/a2ui_adk/) | Connects the agent SDK to the [Agent Development Kit (ADK)](https://github.com/google/adk-python). | [![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/a2ui-adk.svg)](https://pypi.org/project/a2ui-adk/) | ### TypeScript | Package | Description | Version | | --------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | [@a2ui/web_core](typescript/core/web_core/) | Protocol messages, state management, expressions, and basic catalog shared by renderers and `@a2ui/agent`. | [![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@a2ui/web_core.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@a2ui/web_core) | | [@a2ui/lit](typescript/renderers/lit/) | Lit (web components) renderer. | [![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@a2ui/lit.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@a2ui/lit) | | [@a2ui/angular](typescript/renderers/angular/) | Angular renderer. | [![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@a2ui/angular.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@a2ui/angular) | | [@a2ui/react](typescript/renderers/react/) | React renderer. | [![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@a2ui/react.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@a2ui/react) | | [@a2ui/markdown-it](typescript/renderers/markdown-it/) | Markdown rendering with markdown-it and DOMPurify, shared by the web renderers. | [![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@a2ui/markdown-it.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@a2ui/markdown-it) | | [@a2ui/agent](typescript/agents/a2ui_agent/) | Agent SDK: negotiates catalogs, generates prompts and skills, and compiles model output into A2UI. | [![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@a2ui/agent.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@a2ui/agent) | | [@a2ui/catalog-mcp](typescript/catalogs/mcp/) | MCP catalog: calls MCP tools and renders A2UI messages returned in tool results and UI resources. | [![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/@a2ui/catalog-mcp.svg)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@a2ui/catalog-mcp) | | [@a2ui/catalog-vegachart](typescript/catalogs/vegachart/) | VegaChart catalog: renders Vega and Vega-Lite chart specifications on A2UI surfaces. | Not published yet | ### Dart and Flutter | Package | Description | Version | | ---------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | [a2ui_core](dart/a2ui_core/) | Protocol messages, data model, data binding, and expressions for renderers and agents. | [![pub](https://img.shields.io/pub/v/a2ui_core.svg)](https://pub.dev/packages/a2ui_core) | | [a2ui_agent](dart/a2ui_agent/) | Agent SDK: negotiates catalogs, generates prompts and skills, and compiles model output into A2UI. | [![pub](https://img.shields.io/pub/v/a2ui_agent.svg)](https://pub.dev/packages/a2ui_agent) | | [a2ui_flutter](dart/a2ui_flutter/) | Flutter renderer. | [![pub](https://img.shields.io/pub/v/a2ui_flutter.svg)](https://pub.dev/packages/a2ui_flutter) | | [a2ui_cli](dart/a2ui_cli/) | Developer tool that generates typesafe component code from a catalog. | [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/a2ui-project/a2ui/releases) | ### Swift The Swift libraries are distributed via Swift Package Manager from [Package.swift](Package.swift) at the root of this repository. | Package | Description | | -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | | [A2UISwiftCore, BasicCatalog](swift/core/) | Message processor, data model, expression evaluation, and basic catalog definitions. | | [A2UISwiftUI, BasicCatalogSwiftUI](swift/swiftui/) | SwiftUI renderer and basic catalog views. | ## Roadmap - **Protocol v1.1**: We are collecting requirements for the next iteration of the A2UI protocol. - **Inference**: Support for decision models (e.g. Jev). - **Templates**: A cross-framework templating engine and a set of standard primitives for rendering reusable rich UI widgets. - **Sandboxed logic**: A way to securely attach logic to A2UI components. - **Agent SDK**: Skill generation, better diagnostics, and integrations with more agent frameworks. - **Evals**: A set of tools for evaluating generated UI quality. - **MCP Apps**: Embedding MCP Apps inside A2UI, and embedding A2UI experiences into MCP Apps. - **CLI**: Schema validation, codegen, local preview, and integration with coding agents. ## Contribute A2UI is an **Apache 2.0** licensed project. We believe the future of UI is agentic, and we want to work with you to help build it. See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) for details on how to get started.

repositories.description: The workspace to stay in the loop and on top of agents - shape, decide, plan, annotate, review code, share with team, and send all feedback to agents with one click.
repositories.readme:
Everything you need to annotate and stay in the loop with your agents
Inbox Surface • Artifacts • Code Review
Annotate plans, specs, markdown, HTML, and other interactive artifacts. Review diffs and PRs. Send feedback to your agent.

                       

Plannotator Inbox · Official site · Code Review · Visual HTML Skills · Herdr Annotate · (Legacy) Plan Mode

# Plannotator **⭐️ NEW:** [Plannotator Inbox](https://plannotator.ai/inbox/) is the missing review layer between you and multi-agent work. It surfaces decisions, prototypes, variations, plans, and everything you need to stay in the loop. Works with all coding agents and personal assistants. Plannotator is a local, browser-based review surface for AI coding agents: Claude Code, Codex, Copilot CLI, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Kiro, Droid, Amp, DeepSeek Harness, and Pi. Plannotator Inbox also works with personal assistants (Grok Bot, Muse, Hermes, OpenClaw). **It plugs directly into your agent** through plugins, hooks and commands. When the agent proposes a decision, plan, html, or finishes working, the app opens in your browser and you mark it up, comment, and send feedback directly to the agent for it to act on it.
### Review documents, plans, and agent messages Annotate plans, specs, messages, html, then send the feedback to your agent.

Demo: Plan review with Pi
### Code Review Review local changes or remote PRs. Comment on diffs, suggest code. Your comments go back to the agent. Works with Git, GitButler, Jujutsu (`jj`), Perforce (`p4`), GitHub, and GitLab.

AI built in: ask AI about anything you're reviewing,
or launch AI reviews that post comments to the diff.

## Annotate HTML Artifacts

## Plannotator Inbox

The Plannotator Inbox is one local window where your agents leave you messages, questions, files, and guided reviews while they keep working. Answer a question with a click, annotate a file, and press Send when you can. Nothing holds an agent session open while you do, and your reply goes back to the session that asked. ``` plannotator inbox ``` Claude Code, Pi, and OpenCode connect through Plannotator's plugins, and your replies arrive as their next turn. Any other agent reaches it over MCP with `plannotator inbox mcp`, and `plannotator inbox --help` is the guide an agent reads. [Watch the demo](https://plannotator.ai/assets/inbox-film.mp4) · [More on the Inbox](https://plannotator.ai/inbox/) · [Docs](https://plannotator.ai/docs/reference/inbox/) ## Herdr Annotate: Plannotator in the Terminal

  

[Herdr Annotate](https://github.com/plannotator/herdr-annotate) brings Plannotator-style review to the terminal: annotate terminal text, review whole Markdown documents and your coding agent's replies inside [Herdr](https://herdr.dev), and send the feedback straight back to the agent as its next message. Works with Claude Code, Codex, Pi, Copilot CLI, and Droid replies. Annotations are saved in the Plannotator data directory, so terminal reviews and app reviews compound. ``` herdr plugin install plannotator/herdr-annotate ``` Prefer it standalone? [Plannotator TUI](https://github.com/plannotator/plannotator-tui) powers the document review and runs without Herdr: `brew install plannotator/tap/plannotator-tui`. --- ## Commands On Codex, swap the slash commands for `!plannotator …` (e.g. `!plannotator review`) or the `$plannotator-*` skills. ### Annotate ``` /plannotator-annotate README.md # Local markdown file /plannotator-annotate src/ # Browse and annotate files in a folder /plannotator-annotate https://docs.rs/… # Fetch and annotate any URL /plannotator-annotate report.html --render-html # Render HTML as-is instead of converting /plannotator-last # Annotate the agent's last message ``` Need a realistic document to try? Copy the [product requirements document template and filled example](https://docs.plannotator.ai/templates/product-requirements-document) as Markdown. ### Code review ``` /plannotator-review # Review uncommitted changes /plannotator-review # Review a GitHub pull request /plannotator-review # Review a GitLab merge request plannotator review --gitbutler # Review an active GitButler workspace plannotator review --patch-file reading.diff # Review a static caller-supplied unified diff ``` GitButler users can review the whole workspace, one stack, or one branch layer. See the [GitButler workflow guide](https://docs.plannotator.ai/open-source/workflows/gitbutler). ### Plan mode No command needed. Plan mode is wired in through each harness's hooks. Any time your agent creates a plan, the markdown review surface opens for you. ### CLI ``` plannotator sessions # List active Plannotator sessions plannotator sessions --open 1 # Reopen a session in the browser plannotator archive # Browse saved plan decisions read-only ``` --- ## Privacy and network behavior Plannotator does not collect usage telemetry or analytics. Plans, diffs, annotations, drafts, history, and configuration stay local by default. Each plan review, annotate, archive, share-portal, and code-review app surface checks GitHub for the latest Plannotator release when it loads. This sends no plan or review content and gives the Plannotator project owner no usage analytics, although GitHub receives an ordinary request. There is currently no opt-out setting for the release check. Local Git code review can also query the configured `origin` with `git ls-remote` to detect the default branch and a stale baseline; it does not send the local diff. That remote query runs when the review opens, when the page loads its diff, when you switch the diff type or base (including the "Diff out of date · Refresh" button), and when you press Fetch — never on a timer, so an idle review page makes no network calls. Turn it off entirely with `plannotator review --no-git-remote-check`, `PLANNOTATOR_GIT_REMOTE_CHECK=0`, or `{ "gitRemoteCheck": false }` in `~/.plannotator/config.json`; the compare target then comes from local refs only and the "behind GitHub" banner never appears. Content leaves the local workflow only when a network feature needs it: - URL annotation fetches the requested site, through Jina Reader by default for public pages or directly when Jina is disabled or unavailable. - GitHub and GitLab review uses your authenticated CLI and Git remote to retrieve PR or MR data. - Ask AI and review agents send the selected question and relevant plan, document, repository, or diff context to your configured provider. When Ask AI is answered by the agent session that opened Plannotator ("Ask this session"), the question goes to that session instead. - Sharing sends the complete link to whoever or whatever service you use to deliver it. Encrypted short links upload ciphertext to the paste service. - Workspaces is a separate hosted product, so the open source app's local-storage model does not apply to content placed there. The [privacy policy](https://plannotator.ai/privacy) documents these boundaries and the hosted website and waitlist data. --- ## Link sharing Open source asynchronous link sharing remains available for compatibility but is moving to deprecated support. Workspaces is the primary direction for team sharing. No removal date has been announced.

Legacy link-sharing demo: room.plannotator.ai

Share a plan with a teammate and they can annotate it themselves. Import their feedback and send it straight back to your agent. **Small markdown shares** are compressed into the URL fragment. The fragment is not included in the browser's request to the share portal, but it is not encrypted. Anyone or any messaging service with the complete link can read the shared content. The portal host still receives ordinary request metadata. **Large markdown and raw HTML shares** use a short-link service. The share payload is encrypted with AES-256-GCM before upload, the server stores only ciphertext, and the key is kept in the URL fragment rather than sent in the paste request. Anyone with the complete link can decrypt it. Hosted pastes expire after 7 days. Same model as [PrivateBin](https://privatebin.info/). The paste service is [self-hostable](https://docs.plannotator.ai/open-source/workflows/sharing). Sharing can be disabled entirely with `PLANNOTATOR_SHARE=disabled`. [Workspaces](https://plannotator.ai/workspaces) is the primary path for hosted team collaboration. --- ## Install One installer covers almost every agent. It installs the `plannotator` binary, auto-detects your installed agents, and configures hooks, skills, and slash commands for each: ```bash # macOS / Linux / WSL curl -fsSL https://plannotator.ai/install.sh | bash ``` ```powershell # Windows PowerShell irm https://plannotator.ai/install.ps1 | iex ``` The installer downloads the binary from GitHub Releases. A full install can also contact GitHub for release resolution and agent files, Ataraxy-Labs/sem for the optional `sem` sidecar, and npm for Pi, selected extra skills, or the managed agent-terminal runtime. Pinning `--version` skips only GitHub API release resolution, not the release download. See the [privacy policy](https://plannotator.ai/privacy) for the complete network boundaries. Want just the binary and nothing else? Pass `--minimal` (or export `PLANNOTATOR_MINIMAL=1`) to install only the `plannotator` binary to `~/.local/bin`, skipping every skill, hook, slash command, and per-agent config: ```bash curl -fsSL https://plannotator.ai/install.sh | bash -s -- --minimal ``` Then finish the step for your agent: | Agent | After the installer | Details | |---|---|---| | **Amp** | Copy [`plannotator.ts`](apps/amp-plugin/plannotator.ts) into `~/.config/amp/plugins/`, then `plugins: reload`. Workflows live in the command palette. | [README](apps/amp-plugin/README.md) | | **Claude Code** | `/plugin marketplace add backnotprop/plannotator`, then `/plugin install plannotator@plannotator`. Restart Claude Code. | [README](apps/hook/README.md) | | **Codex** | Nothing. Plan review is enabled automatically via Codex's experimental `Stop` hook (macOS/Linux/WSL; on native Windows, Codex hooks are experimental and the installer prints manual setup steps). `$plannotator-review`, `$plannotator-annotate`, and `$plannotator-last` skills included. | [README](apps/codex/README.md) | | **Copilot CLI** | `/plugin marketplace add backnotprop/plannotator`, then `/plugin install plannotator-copilot@plannotator`. Restart. Plan review activates in plan mode (`Shift+Tab`). | [README](apps/copilot/README.md) | | **DeepSeek Harness** | Add `@plannotator/dsh` on DSH's Plugins page, or run `dsh plugin --profile add @plannotator/dsh`. Plan review opens on `exit_plan_mode`. The plugin adds `/plannotator-review`, `/plannotator-annotate` and `/plannotator-last`, which open without blocking the session. | [README](apps/dsh-plugin/README.md) | | **Droid** | `droid plugin marketplace add https://github.com/backnotprop/plannotator`, then `droid plugin install plannotator@plannotator`. Commands only, no plan interception yet. | [README](apps/droid-plugin/README.md) | | **Gemini CLI** | Nothing. The hook, policy, and slash commands are configured automatically. Requires Gemini CLI 0.36.0+. | [README](apps/gemini/README.md) | | **Kiro CLI** | Nothing. Skills and an example agent are installed automatically. Try `kiro-cli chat --agent plannotator`. | [README](apps/kiro-cli/README.md) | | **OpenCode** | Add `"plugin": ["@plannotator/opencode@latest"]` to `opencode.json`. Restart OpenCode. | [README](apps/opencode-plugin/README.md) | | **Pi** | Skip the installer. Just `pi install npm:@plannotator/pi-extension`. Start Pi with `--plan`, or toggle with `/plannotator-plan-mode`. | [README](apps/pi-extension/README.md) | | **T3 Code** | For Claude threads in T3: run `plannotator t3 --help` and follow its two steps (sign in to T3 once, add the `--t3` MCP entry). Your Inbox replies then arrive in the thread as new turns. | [README](packages/t3-code/README.md) | **Updating:** run the installer again for the binary and slash commands. It also updates an installed Claude Code plugin when the `claude` command is on your PATH (opt out with `--skip-claude-plugin`); otherwise run `claude plugin marketplace update plannotator`, then `claude plugin update plannotator@plannotator`, then restart Claude Code (refreshing the marketplace alone does not update the plugin). Pi: `pi update --extensions` (a plain `pi update` updates only Pi). On Claude Code 2.1.287 or newer, plan review, code review and annotate don't make Claude wait: Claude ends its turn and your decision arrives later as a message. Set `PLANNOTATOR_CLAUDE_MOD=0` to go back to the classic flow. Full walkthroughs live in the [installation docs](https://docs.plannotator.ai/open-source/start/installation). ### Uninstall The safe default removes recognized Plannotator-installed components and keeps your local plans, history, drafts, guides, and settings: ```bash plannotator uninstall ``` Use `--purge` for a full removal of known local Plannotator data as well: ```bash plannotator uninstall --purge ``` Purge requires typing `purge` at the prompt and explains that the data is local-only: it is not stored on a Plannotator server and cannot be recovered. For automation, pass `--yes` (or `-y`); non-interactive removal refuses to run without it. Use `--dry-run` to preview recognized work without making changes. Host integrations are always part of uninstall. If a broken or unavailable host prevents safe cleanup, the command names the blocking plugin manager or configuration, gives exact manual cleanup instructions, and stops before deleting the binary. Complete that cleanup and rerun uninstall. It also keeps the binary when an agent's config file can't be read (another tool's too), or when a hook it did not install still runs Plannotator. The error names the file, the tool, and what to do. A `plannotator-inbox` entry you added yourself, or a Claude Code or Droid plugin installed for one project, is named with how to remove it and does not keep the binary. These mechanics keep the ordinary confirmation default-negative, make the irreversible outcome require a stronger explicit word, and still give package managers and scripts a conventional non-interactive flag. The command covers the conventional macOS, Linux, WSL, and Windows binary locations; the managed `sem` sidecar and agent-terminal runtime; installer skills, commands, hooks, policies, caches, and recognizable Amp/Kiro files; and detected Claude Code, Copilot CLI, Droid, Pi, and VS Code installations through their host CLIs. Shared JSONC settings are edited surgically, while strict JSON updates preserve the file's indentation, line endings, and trailing-newline style. Custom or unrecognized files, separately installed optional skills, project-local integrations, external plan-save locations, and invalid configs are preserved (malformed host config is a fail-safe error). If cleanup reports an error, the CLI remains available for a safe retry, and its Windows PATH entry is retained or restored when possible. If PATH restoration itself fails, the output gives the full CLI path for retry and asks for manual PATH repair. For safety, purge refuses filesystem roots, the home directory, the shared temporary directory, symlinked data directories, and non-directory data paths. Existing paths are compared by filesystem identity, so case aliases, symlinks, hardlinks, and bind mounts cannot bypass the root/home/ancestor checks. That identity and every containment guard are revalidated after awaited host commands, immediately before the synchronous data-removal block; a replaced data directory is refused without touching either the old or replacement data. If your dedicated data directory is symlinked, point `PLANNOTATOR_DATA_DIR` at its resolved target and retry. If you installed only the standalone Pi extension and do not have the `plannotator` CLI, use `pi remove npm:@plannotator/pi-extension`.
Claude Code: manual hook setup (without the plugin system) Add to `~/.claude/settings.json`: ```json { "hooks": { "PermissionRequest": [ { "matcher": "ExitPlanMode", "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "command": "plannotator", "timeout": 345600 } ] } ] } } ```
Pin a specific version ```bash curl -fsSL https://plannotator.ai/install.sh | bash -s -- --version vX.Y.Z ``` ```powershell & ([scriptblock]::Create((irm https://plannotator.ai/install.ps1))) -Version vX.Y.Z ```
### Try it The fastest way to see what Plannotator does is to invoke it yourself, right now, from your agent: ``` /plannotator-last # annotate the agent's last reply /plannotator-review # review your current diff, PR-style /plannotator-annotate report.html # annotate any file, folder, or URL ``` (Slash commands in most agents; `$plannotator-*` skills in Codex, command palette in Amp.) Plan review needs no command at all. The next time your agent proposes a plan, it opens in your browser automatically. --- ## How it works ### Plan review ``` Agent calls ExitPlanMode -> PermissionRequest hook fires -> Local server reads plan from hook input -> Browser opens with review UI -> You annotate and approve/deny -> Approve: agent proceeds -> Deny: structured feedback sent to agent -> Agent revises, plan diff shows what changed ``` ### Code review ``` You run /plannotator-review -> git diff captures changes (or PR fetched by URL) -> Browser opens with diff viewer -> Annotate lines, stage/unstage files -> Send feedback: returned to agent session -> Approve: "LGTM" sent ``` --- ## Integrations **VS Code**: Open plans in editor tabs, view diffs inline, add annotations from the editor gutter. Install from the [VS Code Marketplace](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=backnotprop.plannotator-webview). **Obsidian**: Auto-save approved plans to a vault with YAML frontmatter, tags from the plan title, and backlinks for graph connectivity. Configure in Plannotator's Settings panel. **Bear**: Save plans as Bear notes with nested tags and project metadata. **Notion**: Save plans as Markdown child pages under a shared Notion page. Set `NOTION_TOKEN` in the environment that starts Plannotator, then configure the parent page in Settings. **GitHub / GitLab**: Pass any PR or MR URL to `/plannotator-review` and review it with the full diff viewer, annotations, and file tree. --- ## Remote / SSH / devcontainer Plannotator auto-detects SSH sessions and switches to fixed port `19432`. For a different port, or in a devcontainer or Docker: ```bash export PLANNOTATOR_REMOTE=1 export PLANNOTATOR_PORT=9999 # forward this port ``` VS Code devcontainers forward the port automatically (check the Ports tab). For raw SSH, add this to `~/.ssh/config`, using your `PLANNOTATOR_PORT` value if you set one: ``` Host your-server LocalForward 19432 localhost:19432 ``` In remote mode the server listens on every interface (`0.0.0.0`) with no login, so anyone who can reach the port can use it, even when you use an SSH tunnel. Keep the port closed to networks you don't trust. --- ## Security Every released binary ships with a SHA256 sidecar. [SLSA provenance](https://slsa.dev/) attestations are available from v0.17.2. The current release workflow also attaches a CycloneDX JSON SBOM, evaluates it with a fresh Grype database before anything is attested or published, and creates a GitHub/Sigstore SBOM attestation for the shipped binaries and npm tarballs. The SBOM is intentionally labeled as a release-wide Syft inventory of the monorepo's locked build inputs and dependencies. It is not an exact per-binary runtime inventory: Bun standalone executables do not expose their bundled JavaScript package metadata to Syft. The canonical [installation and verification docs](https://docs.plannotator.ai/open-source/start/installation#pin-or-verify-a-release) cover the existing installer path; the exact new SBOM commands are included below and must be copied to that Mintlify page before the first SBOM-enabled release. The release gate rejects scanner-side ignored matches and treats unknown applicability conservatively as runtime when evaluating CISA KEV and fixable Critical findings. Its explicit Grype configuration, complete JSON results, database status, and repository policy decision remain available as workflow evidence. To verify a released Linux x64 binary, its existing provenance, and the new SBOM evidence directly: ```bash tag=vX.Y.Z version="${tag#v}" mkdir -p /tmp/plannotator-release-verify gh release download "$tag" --repo backnotprop/plannotator \ --pattern 'plannotator-linux-x64*' \ --pattern "plannotator-${version}-release-sbom.cdx.json*" \ --dir /tmp/plannotator-release-verify (cd /tmp/plannotator-release-verify && sha256sum --check plannotator-linux-x64.sha256) (cd /tmp/plannotator-release-verify && sha256sum --check "plannotator-${version}-release-sbom.cdx.json.sha256") gh attestation verify /tmp/plannotator-release-verify/plannotator-linux-x64 \ --repo backnotprop/plannotator --source-ref "refs/tags/$tag" \ --signer-workflow backnotprop/plannotator/.github/workflows/release.yml \ --predicate-type https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1 gh attestation verify /tmp/plannotator-release-verify/plannotator-linux-x64 \ --repo backnotprop/plannotator --source-ref "refs/tags/$tag" \ --signer-workflow backnotprop/plannotator/.github/workflows/release.yml \ --predicate-type https://cyclonedx.org/bom ``` These are separate claims over the same artifact digest: provenance identifies its builder/source/workflow, while the CycloneDX predicate describes the release-wide inventory. The release runbook also canonicalizes the downloaded SBOM and attested predicate with `jq -S` and compares them. To verify on install: ```bash curl -fsSL https://plannotator.ai/install.sh | bash -s -- --verify-attestation ``` Requires the `gh` CLI, but no login: the installer fetches the attestation bundle from GitHub's public attestations API and verifies it with `gh attestation verify --bundle` (the extraction needs node, python3, or jq on PATH; gh's authenticated fetch is the fallback). Can also be set persistently in `~/.plannotator/config.json`: ```json { "verifyAttestation": true } ``` Installer verification remains opt-in and verifies SLSA build provenance; normal installation does not require `gh`. See the [canonical installation docs](https://docs.plannotator.ai/open-source/start/installation#pin-or-verify-a-release) for details. --- ## Configuration Settings are saved in cookies (not localStorage) because each hook invocation runs on a random port. You can also set options through environment variables or `~/.plannotator/config.json`. ### Optional Vim controls Plan and annotate views offer a default-off **Vim controls** profile under **Settings → Vim**. Once enabled, focus the document and use `j` / `k` to move one rendered block at a time. After `l` refines into a semantic level, `j` / `k` move among sibling rows, cells, or inline targets; `h` moves back to the containing target. Refining past the deepest target enters text. `v` starts characterwise Visual selection and `V` selects whole blocks. `Space` opens the normal annotation toolbar; `c`, `d`, `m`, and `t` select comment, redline, markup, and label actions. The same semantic target graph drives pointer Pinpoint and keyboard navigation. Press `?` in the document for the contextual key reference. Inputs, dialogs, editors, `Tab`, and all pointer interactions retain their native behavior. The document takes focus automatically when the page is otherwise neutral; press `Escape` from app chrome to return to it without clicking. An additional default-off **Vim HUD** toggle appears beneath Vim controls. It uses the product-demo styling for the live target reticle and navigation context. Its bottom-right **Key panel** is independently hideable while the reticle remains active; `?` still opens the complete key map on demand. The panel shows recent handled keys, the current block/line/word/Visual phase, and the command meaning without capturing text typed into comments or other controls. See [Vim controls](docs/vim-controls.md) for the interaction contract and implementation architecture. | Variable | Description | |---|---| | `PLANNOTATOR_REMOTE` | `1`/`true` for remote mode, `0`/`false` for local, unset for SSH auto-detection | | `PLANNOTATOR_PORT` | Fixed port (default: random locally, `19432` remote) | | `PLANNOTATOR_BROWSER` | Custom browser to open plans in. `none` (also `false`, `0`, `off`, `no`, `true`, `1`, `:`) opens no browser at all; the session URL is always printed. | | `PLANNOTATOR_AI` | `disabled` to disable Ask AI, Review Agents, and Guided Review; the annotate agent terminal is separate | | `PLANNOTATOR_SHARE` | `disabled` to turn off URL sharing | | `PLANNOTATOR_SHARE_URL` | Custom base URL for share links (self-hosted portal) | | `PLANNOTATOR_PASTE_URL` | Base URL of the paste service API | | `PLANNOTATOR_ORIGIN` | Override agent detection: `claude-code`, `amp`, `droid`, `opencode`, `codex`, `copilot-cli`, `gemini-cli`, `kiro-cli`, `pi` | | `PLANNOTATOR_JINA` | `0`/`false` to disable Jina Reader for URL annotation | | `JINA_API_KEY` | Jina Reader API key for higher rate limits | | `PLANNOTATOR_DATA_DIR` | Base directory for Plannotator-managed files (plans, history, drafts, `config.json`). Default: `~/.plannotator`; if that directory doesn't exist and `$XDG_DATA_HOME` is set to an absolute path, `$XDG_DATA_HOME/plannotator` is used instead (also when `~/.plannotator` holds none of Plannotator's data but the XDG folder does). `plannotator data-dir` prints the folder in use | Plannotator-managed files live under `~/.plannotator` by default. Some UI preferences are stored in functional browser cookies. To relocate the files (for example, for an XDG-clean home): ```bash export PLANNOTATOR_DATA_DIR=~/.local/share/plannotator ``` --- ## Development ```bash bun install bun run dev:hook # Plan review server bun run dev:review # Code review editor bun run dev:marketing # Marketing site (plannotator.ai) bun run dev:vscode # VS Code extension (watch mode) ``` ### Build ```bash bun run build # Main targets (hook + opencode + dsh) bun run build:hook # Single-file HTML for the hook server bun run build:review # Code review editor bun run build:opencode # OpenCode plugin bun run build:dsh # DeepSeek Harness plugin bun run build:vscode # VS Code extension ``` Build order matters. The hook build copies pre-built HTML from `apps/review/dist/`. If you change UI code in `packages/ui/`, `packages/editor/`, or `packages/review-editor/`, rebuild the review app first: ```bash bun run --cwd apps/review build && bun run build:hook ``` Test the plugin locally: ```bash claude --plugin-dir ./apps/hook ``` Full binary build: ```bash bun run --cwd apps/review build && bun run build:hook && \ bun build apps/hook/server/index.ts --compile --outfile ~/.local/bin/plannotator ``` --- ## License Copyright 2025-2026 backnotprop Dual-licensed under [Apache 2.0](LICENSE-APACHE) or [MIT](LICENSE-MIT) at your option. Contributions are dual-licensed under the same terms unless you explicitly state otherwise.

repositories.name: dbdelve
repositories.description: Fast and lightweight DB Client made in Rust and GPUI.
repositories.readme: # DBDelve A fast, native, cross-platform, multi-engine database client. Written in Rust with GPUI, no Electron and no JVM: instant startup, friendly on your memory, and smooth scrolling through large tables where other clients crash or introduce limits. ## Community Ideas and discussion on [Discord](https://discord.gg/7PegWzwqCm). ![DBDelve in Gruvbox Dark Glass: a SELECT on the events table in the editor and its result grid below](assets/screenshots/query-dark.png) ![DBDelve in Gruvbox Light Glass: a join in the editor and its result grid below](assets/screenshots/query-light.png) Scrolling a million rows: https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/6e15d566-a110-46c6-a236-52af7d877d4c Launching, with the last results already there: https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/9e55da56-8577-43e0-812a-c77eb5d0e701 ## Why I wanted something which is performant, modern and consumes little ram. The existing DB clients are either filled with bloat (Electron and JVM) or paid. This is an alternative to them. No feature is ever going behind a paywall and with time we will have complete parity on features with those too. ## Install **macOS** (Apple Silicon, macOS 12 or later): ```sh brew install --cask ShayanAbbas1/dbdelve/dbdelve ``` The app isn't notarized, so the cask clears the quarantine flag macOS would otherwise refuse it over. Without Homebrew: ```sh curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ShayanAbbas1/dbdelve/main/install.sh | sh ``` **Linux** (x86_64 or aarch64): the same one-liner installs it under `~/.local` with no root, or `yay -S dbdelve-bin` from the AUR, or the tarball or AppImage from [the latest release][releases]. **Windows** (x86_64): run the installer from [the latest release][releases], or unzip the zip and run `dbdelve.exe`. The installer asks for AppData (just for you) or Program Files (all users). Updating, the `.dmg`, Linux requirements, building from source and where your data lives are all in [docs/install.md](docs/install.md). [releases]: https://github.com/ShayanAbbas1/dbdelve/releases/latest ## Supported databases Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, SQLite, Turso, DuckDB, Snowflake, SQL Server, MongoDB, Redis (and Valkey, KeyDB, Dragonfly) and ClickHouse. Any other database with an ODBC driver is reachable through the bundled ODBC bridge, with that driver installed: IBM Db2, Oracle, SAP HANA, SAP ASE (Sybase), Informix, Teradata, Vertica, Exasol, Firebird, Amazon Redshift, Google BigQuery, Databricks, Apache Hive, Trino and Presto, Dremio, InterSystems IRIS, Microsoft Access and more. Grid editing is off, and statements you type run under the connection's mode. See [Connecting through ODBC](docs/odbc.md). ![The welcome screen: paste a connection URL or pick one of the engines, import from DBeaver or TablePlus, or pick a theme](assets/screenshots/welcome.png) ## What it does - **Make it yours.** The app's own themes alongside Catppuccin, Tokyo Night, Gruvbox and Dracula, each in dark, light and glass. Import themes from Zed or VS Code, or [write your own](docs/themes.md). ![The theme picker, with themes imported from Zed and VS Code and the import commands below them](assets/screenshots/themes.png) - **Bring your connections with you.** Import every saved connection, passwords and SSH settings included, from DBeaver, or TablePlus on macOS. - **Organize your connections into projects,** and jump to any of them from the palette, or disconnect back to a home screen that lists them all. ![The palette scoped to connections, grouped into two projects, with the current connection marked](assets/screenshots/projects.png) - **Never mistake prod for staging.** Every connection is isolated and can color the title bar. Run it read-only, read-write or with full access, and DBDelve asks before anything destructive. ![The connection form, grouped into connection, security and behaviour, with a color and a project for the connection](assets/screenshots/connection-form.png) - **Edits you can read first.** Change a cell and DBDelve writes the `UPDATE` for you to check before it runs. - **Keep the columns you need.** Hide or pin columns, and the layout survives a restart. - **Read a row in full** in the row panel, with JSON highlighted, and edit long values there. ![A table open in the grid, with the row panel showing one row's values and its JSON highlighted](assets/screenshots/table-dark.png) - **Import rows** from CSV, TSV or JSON, with every row checked and every statement shown before anything runs. ![Importing events.csv: format options on the left, each file column mapped to a table column, and a preview of the rows](assets/screenshots/import.png) - **Open a data file** by dropping it on the window: a CSV, Excel, Parquet or JSON file opens in DuckDB, held in memory, as a query you can change. A `.sql` file opens in a new query tab on the connection you're on, and runs only when you run it. - **See the query plan** highlighted in its own pane, with bad row estimates called out. ![An Explain Analyze plan for a join: each node with its actual and estimated rows and time, and a ×76 misestimate flagged](assets/screenshots/query-plan.png) - **Completion that knows your schema:** tables, and a table's columns after its name and a dot. A table is written with an alias, and after `JOIN` with the condition its foreign keys imply. ![Completing accounts. to its columns in a join](assets/screenshots/completion.png) - **Keyboard-first.** One palette for commands, tables, saved queries, history and connections, and every shortcut rebindable. - **Your SSH, not a reimplementation.** Tunnels run through your own `ssh`, so your config, agent and hardware keys just work. For Postgres, a Host that is a directory (`/var/run/postgresql`) reaches that Unix socket on the SSH host, optionally as another user (Run as); the server needs `socat`, and passwordless `sudo` for it when Run as is set. TLS modes other than `disable` and `prefer` are refused there. - **Sign in with a short-lived token.** On Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Redis and ClickHouse, a profile's Password command prints the password at every login, so cloud IAM auth keeps working after the token expires. For Amazon RDS: ```sh /opt/homebrew/bin/aws rds generate-db-auth-token --hostname %HOSTNAME% --port %PORT% --username %USERNAME% --region ``` `%HOSTNAME%`, `%PORT%` and `%USERNAME%` are the profile's own. DBDelve quotes them itself, so write them unquoted: one inside quotes stops the command from running. Give the program's full path (`which aws` prints it): an app opened from the Finder or a desktop launcher does not see the PATH your shell sets. Expires after reuses the output for that many seconds, in memory only; blank runs the command at every login. Free and open source, nothing behind a paywall, and no telemetry: the only request DBDelve makes on its own is an update check, which you can turn off. ## Benchmarks DBDelve 0.3.6 against DBeaver 25.3.1 on the same Postgres table, median of 5 runs each (2026-10-11, M1 Pro, 32 GB): | | DBDelve | DBeaver | | ----------------- | ------- | ------- | | Launch | 1.1 s | 5.2 s | | Idle memory | 133 MB | 606 MB | | 1,000-row query | 0.21 s | 1.96 s | | 1M rows, time | 56 s | 208 s | | 1M rows, memory\* | 4.9 GB | 17 GB | \* The whole 1M-row table pulled into memory on purpose, with the row limit off. Method and full results in [BENCHMARKS.md](BENCHMARKS.md). ## Logs and bug reports DBDelve keeps a diagnostic log on your machine and never sends it anywhere. To attach it to an issue, use **Help → Copy Diagnostics** and paste; **Help → Open Logs Folder** shows the files. If the default log doesn't show the problem, turn on **Verbose logging** in Settings and reproduce it. Read a log before you post it and remove anything sensitive. A verbose one can hold hostnames, database names and anything a database driver logs. ## License Copyright (C) 2026 Shayan Abbas and contributors, licensed under the [GPL-3.0](LICENSE). Code contributed before the switch was released under the [MIT License](licenses/MIT-dbdelve.txt), and that notice still applies to it. Third-party font and theme licenses are in [NOTICES.md](NOTICES.md). ## Sponsors Support DBDelve on [Patreon](https://www.patreon.com/membership/30003257). Sponsors are listed here and on the site. ## Contributors Thank you to everyone who has contributed to DBDelve. Want to join them? Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md).
